The Section on Repentance and Receiving Precepts Based on the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*. **Chapter One: Clarifying the Characteristics of the Bodhisattva Lineage** This chapter clarifies the characteristics of the Bodhisattva lineage. It is derived from the thirty-fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which sets forth six types of lineage for the various *pāramitās* of the Bodhisattvas.
By means of these marks,
others are made to recognize that he is truly a bodhisattva.
First, regarding the marks of the lineage (*gotra*):
That is to say, bodhisattvas are by nature inclined toward generosity;
they are capable of giving in the present,
and they give continuously, impartially, joyfully, and without regret.
Although small, it can be made equal to the vast and not small;
if one has nothing to give,
one feels deep shame and remorse.
He always delights in praising and exhorting others to give;
he finds joy in seeing those who are worthy of offerings.
Respectfully making offerings,
one will have no sinful deeds or harmful matters in this world or the next.
Whether requested or unrequested,
he teaches according to the truth.
Should there be fear of kings, thieves, water, or fire, [he provides protection].
Bestowing fearlessness,
they are able to rescue others from extreme terror according to their capacity.
He never failed to return items entrusted to him by others; even when he incurred debts to others,
[he was diligent in repayment].
He never resists or refuses;
regarding shared property,
he harbors no heart of deception or guile.
Even upon obtaining great wealth and treasures,
they do not become greedily attached to them,
let alone minor gains.
Such as these are called the characteristics of the lineage of generosity.
Regarding the characteristics of the lineage of ethical discipline:
it refers to those bodhisattvas who, by their very nature, possess inferior grades of unwholesome physical, verbal, and mental karma.
He is not excessively violent or cruel toward sentient beings,
nor does he cause them excessive harm or affliction.
Although one has committed evil deeds,
one is able to repent swiftly and constantly practices a sense of shame and remorse.
They do not give rise to joy [in harming others],
nor do they afflict or injure sentient beings with weapons or the like;
by nature, they are always compassionate and loving.
Toward those who are worthy of respect,
one should perform prostrations in their presence and cultivate the practice of harmonious reverence.
He was quick-witted and not dull-witted;
he skillfully conformed to the minds of others and always maintained a smile before speaking.
With a relaxed countenance and level gaze,
one remains free from frowning;
one should be the first to speak and offer greetings.
Recognizing kindness and repaying it;
when others come seeking what is upright and sincere,
one does not respond with flattery or false thanks.
Seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma,
not through what is contrary to the Dharma,
nor by means of violence.
If one joyfully cultivates merit,
one should still encourage others to do so;
how much more so when doing it for oneself?
Hearing of others being oppressed by various sufferings,
one regards them as more intense than one's own; thus, even for a minor transgression, one feels profound fear.
How much more so for those with many offenses.
He performs all activities in accordance with the Dharma and does not follow what is contrary to the Dharma.
Evil thoughts do not continue;
they are abandoned as soon as they arise.
One is virtuous, respectful, truthful, and free from deception.
One does not even speak harshly to one's own servants and attendants,
much less to others.
Such categories as these are called the characteristics of the lineage of ethical discipline (*śīla-gotra*). As for the characteristics of the lineage of patience (*kṣānti-gotra*),
it refers to those bodhisattvas whose nature is such that, when encountering harm from others, [they remain patient].
Without a mind of ill will or harm,
and not retaliating in return, one should accept the apologies of others if they offer them.
They are able to receive [the teaching] swiftly;
they never harbor resentment,
nor do they long maintain malice.
Such categories as these are called the characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*).
As for the characteristic of diligence (*vīrya*),
it refers to the fact that bodhisattvas are by nature inherently alert and energetic.
Rising early and sleeping late,
he took no pleasure in slumber;
in all his actions, he was courageous and resolute.
One delights in non-forgetfulness;
whatever undertakings one performs are firm and brought to completion,
never being interrupted or abandoned.
Possessing great purpose, they are without timidity;
they do not disparage themselves,
and they have the power to realize difficult-to-practice deeds.
Fearless and undaunted, he is able to bring about what is meaningful and beneficial;
even amidst matters of great importance, he never feels profound weariness.
How much more so for minor matters?
Such categories as these are called the characteristics of diligence (*vīrya*).
As for the characteristics of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):

This refers to those bodhisattvas whose nature is such that they are able to contemplate the meaning of the Dharma with thorough discernment and without much distraction; whether seeing or hearing [the teachings],
they dwell in mountain caves, forests, or at the edges of groves, remaining unacquainted with worldly people.
Avoiding evil beings and conforming to silent seclusion,
one then gives rise to love and joy.
Naturally having few afflictions,
he went to a secluded place and contemplated his own welfare.
The mind is not excessively entangled or disturbed by evil discursive thoughts;
it maintains even loving-kindness toward enemies,
let alone toward friends or neutral persons.
Seeing suffering, he gave rise to compassion;
according to his capacity, he rescued and delivered others.
By nature, he was intelligent and quick-witted.
One is able to receive, uphold, and contemplate the Dharma;
having long practiced it, one both recalls it oneself and causes others to recall it as well.
Such categories as these are called the characteristics of the lineage of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
As for the characteristics of the lineage of wisdom (*prajñā*),
it refers to the innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*) possessed by all bodhisattvas.
They are able to enter the spheres of all fields of knowledge;
their nature is not dull or obscure,
even regarding objects of heedlessness.
It possesses the power of analytical discernment;
such categories as these are called the lineage of wisdom.
It is by virtue of the lineage possessed by all bodhisattvas [that they attain this].
Being endowed with such merits as these,
one accomplishes all virtuous and pure dharmas;
therefore, one attains the rare and unsurpassed state of a Tathāgata.
It serves as the cause for realization;
furthermore, until one is defiled by the four secondary afflictions that are contrary to the white dharmas— whether they are present or absent—
and until those associated with the white dharmas have subsided or are defiled.
In this way, all pure dharmas fail to manifest.
What are the four afflictions that are contrary to these pure dharmas?
They are, namely, heedlessness.
Due to having previously habituated oneself to various afflictions,
one's nature becomes characterized by intense and long-lasting afflictions;
this is called the first [type].
Furthermore, the second [cause] is that those who are foolish and unskilled rely upon evil friends.
Furthermore, being constrained by elders, husbands, kings, thieves, enemies, and so forth,
one lacks autonomy and the mind becomes confused and distracted.
This is called the third.
Furthermore, those who lack the necessities of life will be preoccupied with their own bodies and lives.
This is called the fourth nature of secondary affliction;
although one possesses the spiritual lineage,
it arises due to four causes and conditions.
They will not be able to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
What are these four? They are:
first, that various bodhisattvas have not previously encountered Buddhas, bodhisattvas, or true spiritual friends who can explain to them the unerring path to bodhi.
This is called the first cause.
Furthermore, although bodhisattvas may encounter virtuous friends who explain the true path to them,
they maintain perverted attachments.
To practice erroneously regarding that which one is correctly training in is called the second cause.
Furthermore, although bodhisattvas may encounter virtuous friends who explain the correct path and enable them to train correctly, [they may still fail].
Furthermore, regarding the preparatory application of skillful means,
being lax and unable to exert oneself with fierce and ardent diligence is called the third cause.

Furthermore, although various bodhisattvas may encounter virtuous friends who explain the path of right practice to them, they lack the vigor for application because their roots of goodness have not yet matured.
The fact that the provisions have not yet been perfected and that one has not practiced the factors conducive to enlightenment for a long period of time is called the fourth cause.
The Section Clarifying the Causes and Conditions for Arousing the Mind. Regarding those who arouse the mind of bodhi,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind," states that there are briefly five kinds.
First, intrinsic nature;
second, aspect;
third, object-condition.
The four virtues and the five excellences of the bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind of awakening.
Regarding all the correct aspirations of bodhisattvas,
this initial correct aspiration is able to universally encompass all other correct aspirations;
therefore, the generation of the mind has this initial correct aspiration as its essential nature.
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of right aspiration and seek enlightenment,
they conceive such thoughts and speak these words:
May I certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
may I be able to accomplish all that is beneficial for sentient beings,
and ultimately establish them in final nirvāṇa and the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the arousal of this mind necessarily seeks unsurpassed enlightenment for oneself and seeks to bring about the welfare of sentient beings; therefore,
the arousal of the mind has "necessarily seeking" as its defining characteristic.
Taking great enlightenment and all the aims and benefits of sentient beings as its object of focus,
the initial generation of the mind is able to encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment.
With these sublime roots of goodness as the foremost,
they are thus good and supremely good;
they are wondrous and supremely wondrous.
It is endowed with the merit of exhausting all the bases of the three karmas of sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is the primary correct aspiration generated by Bodhisattvas when they first resolve their minds;
compared to all other excellent, virtuous, and correct aspirations that seek worldly or supramundane goals, [it is supreme].
This is the most supreme.
A bodhisattva’s generation of the mind of awakening arises from four conditions, four causes, and four powers.
First, as for the four conditions:
First, it refers to a son of good family or a daughter of good family who either personally witnesses the inconceivable power of miraculous transformations of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
or hears of such matters from a reliable source.
Having seen and heard this, they then form this thought:
"Unsurpassed Bodhi possesses great merit;
it enables those who abide in it and those who practice it to achieve such inconceivable miraculous transformations, merits, and majestic powers."
By the predominant power of this seeing and hearing,
they develop profound faith and understanding toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*),
and thereby give rise to the mind set on great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
This is called the first [reason]: one should cause them to resolve their minds because this is what can be cultivated and realized by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for which they should be instructed.
Second, although they have not seen or heard of the supernatural powers and meritorious qualities of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
Having heard the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they develop deep faith.
By the power of hearing the true Dharma and by the force of that deep faith,
they give rise to profound conviction and understanding regarding the Tathāgata’s qualities of miraculous transformation, for the sake of attaining the subtle and wondrous wisdom of a Tathāgata.
Prior to generating the bodhicitta, one either perceives it oneself or hears of the miraculous powers and meritorious qualities of other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
whereas the previous account was based on the perception of others regarding the Buddha,
this present account concerns the arising of faith after hearing the teachings.
Third, there may be a certain class of people who,
although they have not seen, heard, or been taught the aforementioned sublime Dharma,
nevertheless see that the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka is on the verge of disappearing.
He then thought: "The Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka shall long abide in the world,
able to uproot the great suffering of immeasurable sentient beings."
I should uphold the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta),
and act for the sake of extinguishing the great suffering of immeasurable sentient beings.
By the predominant power of protecting and upholding the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
they develop profound faith and understanding in the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
and for the sake of attaining the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata.
They resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Fourth, there may be a certain class of persons who,
although they do not witness the extinction of the True Dharma, [still generate this resolve].
Yet, during the final kalpa, the final age, and the final period,
they see sentient beings in a state of turbid evil, their bodies and minds afflicted by the ten secondary afflictions—
namely, that they are largely deluded.
They possess much lack of shame and lack of dread of blame;
they possess much stinginess and envy;
they possess much sorrow and suffering.
There is much heaviness and rigidity;
there is much affliction;
there is much unwholesome conduct.
They are full of negligence, full of indolence,
and full of lack of faith.
Having seen this, he then thought: "In this great, turbid,
and evil world, which has now arisen and is being afflicted and disturbed by various secondary afflictions,
one is able to give rise to the inferior mind of a Pratyekabuddha."
It is already difficult to obtain even that;
how much more so for one who can resolve their mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
I ought to resolve my mind upon great bodhicitta.
I cause immeasurable sentient beings in this degenerate age to follow my example and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment,
because they perceive that generating the resolve for awakening in such a degenerate age requires extraordinary effort.
One develops profound faith and understanding toward great enlightenment;
based on this, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment.
These are called the four conditions.
What are the four causes? They are as follows:
that Bodhisattvas are endowed with the spiritual lineage (gotra);
this is called the first.
Being sustained by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and virtuous friends is called the second;
it is to give rise frequently to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings.
This is called the third:
being without fear or cowardice regarding the great suffering of birth and death and the difficult practices over an exceedingly long period of time.
This is called the fourth.
First, they possess the bodhisattva lineage;
second, they possess the four characteristics.
It should be known that a bodhisattva is endowed with excellent spiritual friends;
that is to say, the spiritual friends encountered by these bodhisattvas are by nature not dull-witted.
Being intelligent and wise,
one does not fall into wrong views;
this is called being fully endowed with the first kind of virtuous friend.
Any virtuous friends they encounter will never teach them to practice heedlessness,
nor will they provide them with any implements of heedlessness.
This is called the second fulfillment of a virtuous friend:
whatever virtuous friends one encounters will never instruct one to engage in unwholesome conduct.
Furthermore, they do not provide them with the requisites for unwholesome conduct;
this is called the third fulfillment of a virtuous friend.
Such is the virtuous friend one encounters.
They never encourage the relinquishing of superior faith, aspiration, training, diligence, skillful means, or meritorious qualities;
rather, they instead encourage the cultivation of inferior faith, aspiration, and all base meritorious qualities.
This means not encouraging the abandonment of the Mahāyāna to practice the two vehicles,
and not encouraging the abandonment of superior merit and wisdom to cultivate inferior merit and wisdom;
this is called the fourth perfection of a spiritual friend.
One should know that bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings due to four causes and conditions.
That is to say, although there are immeasurable and boundless worlds free from suffering throughout the ten directions for the bodhisattvas, [they do not seek rebirth therein].
And they are born into worlds characterized by suffering,
wherein various forms of suffering are constantly encountered;
at times, they even witness others undergoing one form of suffering or another.
At times, one sees oneself encountering a single painful contact;
or one sees oneself and others being oppressed by the encounter with a single painful contact;
or one sees both encountering various kinds of intense, uninterrupted, and great painful contacts for a long duration.
Nevertheless, this bodhisattva, relying on their own spiritual lineage and inherent virtue,
and relying on the four objective spheres, is able to give rise to inferior, middling, and superior compassion, even though they have not practiced them habitually.
Without interruption,
one first gives rise to compassion toward all sentient beings due to four causes and conditions.
Even regarding the great suffering of saṃsāra— various, intense, uninterrupted, and unbroken over an exceedingly long period— and even toward difficult ascetic practices,
they have no fear or dread;
how much less so toward minor sufferings?
That is to say, bodhisattvas are by nature courageous, resilient, and powerful;
this is the first cause.
They are by nature intelligent and capable of correct reflection.
Possessing the power of analytical discernment is the second cause [for being able to attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The third cause is the accomplishment of superior, pure faith and understanding toward all sentient beings.
The accomplishment of a superior, profound mind of compassion is the fourth cause.
These explain the aforementioned four causes in their respective order.
As for the "four powers":
This means that by their own power,
bodhisattvas are able to generate a profound sense of love and delight for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the first [type of attainment],
which occurs regarding great enlightenment through the power of others.
They develop deep affection and delight;
this is called the second [cause]:
having previously practiced wholesome dharmas associated with the Mahāyāna.
Now, by being able to see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas even for a moment,
or by hearing their praises and eulogies even briefly,
one is able to swiftly generate the bodhicitta.
How much more so for one who beholds his supernormal powers and hears his true Dharma;
this is called the third [benefit] in the present life.
Associating with virtuous persons,
hearing the true Dharma, and reflecting upon it correctly, and so forth.
Having cultivated various wholesome dharmas over a long period of time,
one generates the bodhicitta through this application;
this is called the fourth power.
There are four causes and conditions for the regression of the bodhicitta that can cause a bodhisattva to regress from the bodhicitta.
The first is the lack of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second, being influenced by evil friends;
third, having a meager sense of compassion for all sentient beings;
and fourth, regarding the great suffering of saṃsāra over an extremely long period and the practice of difficult austerities.
It means timidity, fear, and terror.
Regarding the Bodhisattva who has firmly resolved upon the initial aspiration for enlightenment— the gateway that reveals supremacy—
there are, in brief, two extraordinary and most marvelous qualities not shared with the world.
What are these two?
First, gathering all sentient beings as one's retinue;
second, being untainted by the faults associated with having a retinue.
There are two kinds of faults regarding the gathering of followers:
namely, providing benefit to or causing harm to those followers.
Defilement, opposition, and compliance—
these two matters are entirely absent in the bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva who has firmly resolved their initial aspiration toward all sentient beings gives rise to two kinds of excellent and superior intentions.
First is the intention for benefit;
second is the intention for happiness.
Regarding the intention for benefit:
That is to say, it is the intention to deliver sentient beings from those various unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states for their peace and happiness.
That is to say, with regard to sentient beings who are destitute, without support, and without protection,
one abandons a defiled mind and desires to provide them with various means of benefit and happiness.
Because a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind seeks awakening,
the wholesome dharmas they encompass possess two kinds of superiority over all other encompassed wholesome dharmas:
first, the cause.
The second fruit refers to the fact that all the wholesome dharmas it encompasses are the causes for realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
and because this unsurpassed state to be realized is its fruit; thus,
it is superior even to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
How much more so for all other worldly causes and effects!
For a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind, there are two kinds of benefits from that resolution.
First, once the initial resolve has been made:
They are the field of merit revered by sentient beings;
all sentient beings should make offerings to them.
Furthermore, they act as the parents of all sentient beings.
Second, having first resolved their mind [on awakening],
they are immediately able to gather the merit of non-affliction and non-harm.
This bodhisattva accomplishes such merit of non-affliction and non-harm.
They obtain the protection guarded by the double wheel-turning kings;
because they are protected by such guardianship, whether they are sleeping,
awake, or in a state of confusion and fainting, [they remain secure].
No demons, malevolent spirits, humans, or non-humans will be able to harass or harm them. Furthermore,
when they pass away from this life and take up another birth, [they shall likewise be protected].
Because they are protected and sustained by such merit,
they have little illness and remain free from disease, never being afflicted by chronic or severe illnesses;
they constantly benefit sentient beings.
Without toil and without loss,
the superior matters are explained in detail.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, Chapter Two.
The bodhisattva’s production of the thought of awakening possesses four kinds of greatness.
First is the greatness of valor,
which refers to the profound and difficult-to-perform diligence of the great vow.
Second is the greatness of skillful means, which refers to donning the armor of the great vow. This is because it accords with [the goal] for a long duration.
Third is the greatness of benefit, because one constantly exerts oneself through skillful means and diligence,
thereby accomplishing the welfare of both oneself and others at all times.
Fourth is the greatness of renunciation;
that is to say, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi,
what serves as the root from which a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment?
As for what constitutes obstacles and hindrances to the ultimate [attainment], etc.,
great compassion is the root,
and benefiting sentient beings is the basis.
Taking the Mahāyāna teachings as the object of faith,
taking omniscience as the object of focus,
and seeking that [omniscience] for its sake.
They take supreme desire as their vehicle,
because they seek the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
they take great protection as their dwelling.
Because they abide by the bodhisattva precepts,
taking the reception of obstacles as a difficulty;
and because they give rise to the mind of other vehicles.
It takes the increase of virtue as its merit;
it takes merit and wisdom as its intrinsic nature;
and it takes the practice of the perfections as its means of transcendence.
Taking the fulfillment of the stages as the ultimate goal,
because one applies diligent skillful means at each stage in accordance with its respective requirements,
starting from the initial conventional generation of the mind.
That which is called "arousing the mind" by hearing, retaining, awakening to, and understanding it from others is termed the conventional arousal of the mind;
this arises through four powers.
First is the arousal of the mind through the power of friends,
meaning that one encounters and accords with virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Second is the power of causes.
Or because their nature was previously established by having generated the resolve for awakening in past lives;
third, the power of the faculties,
because they have been fulfilled through the roots of goodness practiced in the past.
Fourth is the power of hearing.
This is because, when he preaches the Dharma in various places,
immeasurable sentient beings resolve their minds upon bodhicitta.
From the *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Teachings), Chapter Two: On the Worldly Generation of the Mind.
This refers to a certain class of individuals who...
The wise one stands before him with reverence and,
generating a superior resolve, makes this vow:
"Venerable sir, please remember."
Some say "the Venerable One remembers," while others say "the Upādhyāya [remembers]:
I am named so-and-so."
From this day forward,
I shall generate the mind set on unexcelled bodhi for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
From this day forward,
may all the six pāramitās and all my myriad practices that I cultivate be for the sake of realizing unexcelled bodhi.
"I now go forth in harmony with these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
May the World-Honored One bear witness that I am a bodhisattva.
A second and a third time, he spoke thus.
The first, the excellence of the ultimate resolve, has three kinds of excellence:
first, the excellence of instruction,
because of approaching the Truly Perfectly Enlightened One (samyaksaṃbuddha).
Second, superiority in accordance,
because of the thorough accumulation of merit and wisdom;
third, superiority in the attainment of the fruit.
One gives rise to non-conceptual wisdom;
the cultivation and development of this resolve is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
What is the cause of this excellence?
There are four: first, the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*).
Because of the thorough realization of the selflessness of phenomena,
there is the equality of sentient beings;
because of the attainment of the equality of self and others, [there is the equality of the Dharma].
Third is the equality of activity,
because one causes others to exhaust suffering just as one exhausts it oneself.
Fourth is the equality of the Buddha-body.
Because one is able to definitively penetrate the fact that the dharma-realm and the self are non-different,
this first ultimate resolve for awakening (bodhicitta) further possesses six excellences: first,
the excellence of the stage of birth.
Second, the stage of aspiration; third, vigor;
fourth, pure reliance.
Fifth, excellence of skill;
sixth, excellence of emergence.
There are four types of excellence of birth.
First, the excellence of the seed:
having faith in the Great Dharma as the seed.
Second, the excellence of the birth-mother.
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the birth mother,
the three wombs are supreme;
because the bliss of great meditative concentration (*mahādhyāna*) is the womb.
The four nurses are supreme because Great Compassion nurtures one as a nurse;
"vows" refers to the Ten Great Vows.
One should rely on the forty-fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
as explained below:
first, making offerings to and revering all Buddhas.
Second, they uphold all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time.
Third, they go to every place where the Tathāgatas turn the wheel of Dharma to make offerings and listen to the true Dharma.
Fourth, it clarifies the superior practices performed by all bodhisattvas.
Fifth, it brings all sentient beings to maturity,
as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Sixth, thoroughly knowing the realm of vessels and the realm of sentient beings;
seventh, purifying all buddha-fields;
eighth, never being separated from all bodhisattvas and buddhas.
Ninth, benefiting sentient beings,
like a medicinal tree or a wish-fulfilling jewel.
All those born [in his presence] receive benefit.
Tenth, he constantly benefits sentient beings according to their needs, never resting.
This is not like the two vehicles, which enter nirvana swiftly.
Just as there are three types of the foremost offering:
first, [the offering] to all Buddhas without exception.
Second, there are three ways of making offerings without remainder:
first, the offering of benefit.
The first refers to clothing and so forth;
the second refers to respectful offerings,
such as incense and flowers.
Third is the offering of practice,
which refers to cultivating faith, precepts, and so forth;
third is the offering of reverent respect without remainder.
There are three:
first, respectful service;
second, respectful reception.
Third is the cultivation of reverence,
as explained at length in the third chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* establishes the various great vows through ten phrases of ultimate exhaustion (*daśa-paryanta-pada*).
What are the ten? They are as follows:
first, the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings, because all births arise from it.
Second, the exhaustion of the world-realm,
meaning the realm where one dwells.
Third, the exhaustion of the space-realm.
This refers to all of space,
wherein the four dharma-realms are exhausted;
that is to say, it explains what dharmas are taught and what dharmas are used for conversion.
Fifth, the exhaustion of the realms of nirvāṇa,
because they place those beings to be transformed within whichever realm of nirvāṇa is appropriate. Sixth,
the exhaustion of the worlds in which Buddhas appear.
Seventh, the realm of the Tathāgatas’ wisdom is exhausted;
thus, by what skillful means is the Tathāgatas’ wisdom exhausted?
Eighth, the realm of the mind’s objects is exhausted.
Because the mind follows its objects until the realm of objects is exhausted;
the ninth is the exhaustion of the entrance into the realm of the Buddha’s cognitive wisdom.
Furthermore, whichever realm it may be, the entrance into the Buddha’s cognitive wisdom is exhausted.
The wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma throughout the ten worlds pervades the entire realm;
because this aspiration is supreme,
one is courageous and never regresses.
One is able to perform what is difficult to perform because one never regresses.
As for the pure reliance, it arises based on the two benefits.
First, because one knows that awakening is near;
second, because one knows the skillful means for benefiting others;
and third, because one attains superior skillful means for progressing to higher stages.
The Victor’s excellence of renunciation consists in his excellent reflection,
for he abides in the dharmas established within the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the door of praise by means of similes, the verse on the simile for generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*) states:
Like the earth, like pure gold;
like the moon, like a growing fire;
like a treasury, like a jewel casket.
Like the ocean, like a diamond,
like a mountain, like the King of Medicines;
like a friend, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Like the sun, like beautiful music;
like a king, like a treasury;
like a path, like a vehicle.
Like a spring, like a joyful sound,
like a stream, and like clouds— the generation of the mind of awakening is illustrated by these similes.
It is, for example, like the earth.
The initial generation of the mind of awakening is also like this,
for it is able to give rise to and sustain all Buddha-dharmas.
It is, for example, like pure gold.
The same applies to the bodhicitta arising from association,
because it does not regress or perish in its pursuit of the benefit and happiness [of beings];
it is like the new moon.
The arousal of the mind associated with diligence is likewise;
because all wholesome dharmas gradually increase,
it is like an increasing fire.
The generation of the mind of awakening through ultimate reliance and application is likewise.
Because it relies on the culmination of accumulated practices, which are like adding fuel to a fire,
it is compared to a treasury of fire.
The arousal of the mind associated with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is also like this;
because it provides for all with material wealth without exhaustion,
it is like a precious casket.
The arousal of the mind associated with ethical discipline (*śīla*) is likewise;
for the jewels of the qualities of merit arise from it,
just as [jewels arise] from the great ocean.
The generation of the mind associated with the perfection of patience is likewise:
because the mind remains unmoved by all adversities that arise,
it is like a diamond.
The generation of the mind associated with progress is also like this;
because it is courageous, firm, and indestructible,
it is like the king of mountains.
The generation of the mind associated with the dhyāna-pāramitā is also like this:
no thing can move it,
because it is undisturbed.
It is like a king of medicines;
the resolve associated with prajñā is also like this,
for it can destroy the two diseases of affliction and ignorance.
Just as with a virtuous friend,
so too is the generation of the mind associated with immeasurability,
because it does not abandon sentient beings at any time.
For example, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem;
the generation of the mind of awakening associated with supernormal powers is also like this,
for it can accomplish whatever one desires to manifest.
It is like the midday sun;
the mind generated through the application of skillful means is also like this,
for it brings sentient beings to maturity, just as the sun ripens grain.
Just as there is beautiful music,
so too is the bodhicitta that is skillfully applied;
for it teaches the Dharma and transforms sentient beings through gathering them in.
For example, it is like a king;
so too is the bodhicitta that accords with measure,
for it serves as the indestructible cause of the true path.
For example, it is like a granary;
the bodhicitta associated with accumulation is likewise,
for it is the place where the wealth of the dharmas of merit and wisdom is gathered.
It is like a road; the generation of the mind associated with the factors of enlightenment is also like this,
because the Great Sage has already traveled it first and others follow along it.
It is like a vehicle;
the generation of the mind that accords with śamatha and vipaśyanā is also like this,
for it proceeds in peace and security when both wheels are complete.
It is like a gushing spring;
the generation of the mind associated with dhāraṇī is also thus, for although those who hear it are many, [the teaching flows forth inexhaustibly].
Because the Dharma is inexhaustible;
it is like the sound of joy.
The arousal of the mind that accords with the seals of the Dharma is also like this.
Because it is what those seeking liberation delight to hear,
the generation of the mind that accords with its intrinsic nature is like a flowing river.
The path of the patience of non-arising flows spontaneously because there is no volitional effort;
it is like a great cloud.
The same applies to the generation of the mind that accords with worldly skillful means:
it manifests the attainment of enlightenment through the eight phases in order to transform sentient beings.
As stated in the Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra,
there are thirty-two similes;
the bodhisattva has four joys.
First, the joy of contemplating benefit and happiness; that is, when one contemplates the welfare of others.
Second, the joy of attaining skillful means.
This refers to the joy of attaining skillful means;
and the joy of understanding the meaning,
which refers to the time of comprehending the intent of the Mahāyāna.
Fourth is the realization of the bliss of truth.
This refers to when one realizes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
yet abandons sentient beings to pursue solitary extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
It should be understood that such a person does not obtain these four joys of a bodhisattva; this explains the fault of a bodhisattva who has not yet resolved their mind [for enlightenment].
Next, the praise for those who have resolved their minds is stated:
if a bodhisattva first generates the great mind of bodhi, [they attain these joys].
At that time, by relying on infinite sentient beings,
one immediately attains excellent protection and refrains from committing any evil deeds.
For this reason,
such a person is far removed from the fear of falling back into the miserable realms.
Furthermore, it is because of the presence and increase of wholesome qualities.
One always rejoices in pleasure because of the presence and increase of compassion;
one always rejoices in suffering for the same reason.
For this reason,
such a person is far removed from the fear of falling away from the good paths.
Because of this, they give rise to the resolve to maintain non-action— that is, they are able to skillfully guard against committing any evil.
The verse says:
Loving others more than oneself,
one forgets oneself to benefit sentient beings.
One does not hate others for one's own sake;
how could one perform unwholesome deeds?
A bodhisattva loves others more than they love themselves.
For this reason,
one forgets one's own life to benefit others,
and does not harm others for the sake of self-benefit.
For this reason,
they are able to sever all evil karma regarding all sentient beings and attain non-retrogression;
thus, the bodhisattva uses their own merit as their own adornment.
They take delight in benefit as their food;
they take the places of rebirth produced by mental volition as their gardens;
and they take the transformations of supernormal powers as their play and joy.
These four matters exist only for bodhisattvas;
they do not exist for those of the two vehicles.
Since these four conditions exist,
how could there be any regression?
Next, [the text] refutes the thought of mental distress.
Since the bodhisattva takes great compassion as his very essence,
he exerts himself to the utmost for the benefit of others; thus, even when entering the Avīci hell,
it is like visiting a place of recreation.
If this is so for a bodhisattva,
how could they ever give rise to fear regarding other forms of suffering?
Is it because of such fear that their resolve regresses?
For all Bodhisattvas, the preceptor of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) dwells constantly within their hearts;
thus, when they see sentient beings undergoing suffering, [they do not regress].
One thus generates suffering for oneself; by this principle,
one should act spontaneously.
If one must wait for the exhortation of a virtuous friend to be inspired,
one will develop a profound and extremely heavy sense of shame.
As the verse says:
Bearing the burden of sentient beings,
laziness is a disgrace and not superior;
it is for the sake of wishing to untie the bonds of others.
One’s diligence should be a hundredfold.
Since a bodhisattva has resolved their mind upon taking up the heavy burden of sentient beings,
to proceed with laxity would be a disgraceful matter.

It is not for the sake of being the foremost among upright beings that a bodhisattva should reflect upon the various urgent fetters— namely, afflictions, karma, and birth— whether pertaining to oneself or others.
To untie these bonds,
one must apply oneself with a hundredfold diligence toward performing what is to be done, surpassing even the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Next, it is taught that there are six great aspects of conduct that accord with the practice of benefiting both self and others.
"Great reliance" means that one generates the resolve for enlightenment by relying upon great bodhi.
"Great practice" means...
It is for the sake of benefiting oneself and others that one initiates the practice;
it is of great fruit because one now attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Great grasping" means that at the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one embraces all sentient beings.
"Great patience" means...
Regarding "generating" (utpādana): it is because one endures all great sufferings at the time of its production.
Regarding "great purpose" (mahārtha):
it is because at the time of attaining the fruit, the activity of extensively benefiting all sentient beings is accomplished.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of greatness.
First is the greatness of transcendence,
because it transcends the three realms of existence and the five destinies.
Second is the greatness of tranquility,
because it tends toward non-abiding nirvana.
Third is the greatness of merit.

Fourth is the greatness of benefiting others, because one constantly relies on great compassion and does not abandon sentient beings. This is due to the increase of the two accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Based on the initial intent of the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*,
this work praises and exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta,
explaining that the various merits and sublime practices cultivated therein possess remedial power and benefit.
They praise the various merits of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
causing them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment] by saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, if a disciple of the Buddha upholds the words of the Buddha..."
One who is able to expound the Dharma for sentient beings should first extol the virtues of the Buddha; having heard this,
sentient beings will then be able to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
Seeking the wisdom of the Buddha,
by virtue of having resolved their minds,
the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be interrupted.
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās recollect the Buddha and recollect the Dharma,
they further recollect when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, he underwent various hardships and sufferings for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This mind should thus recollect the Buddha’s kindness, thinking: "He sought the Dharma through diligent toil for our sake.
Now, one should act in this way to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Whenever he speaks to others to inspire them to resolve their minds for awakening and practice the bodhisattva path,
he preaches the Dharma to those bodhisattvas— even if it be but a single verse— with such an intention.
When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, which instructs,
exhorts, benefits, and gladdens them,
they shall plant roots of goodness and cultivate the Buddha-dharma.
Having attained unsurpassed enlightenment,
for the sake of severing the various sufferings and afflictions of birth and death that sentient beings have endured since beginningless time,
he desires to accomplish immeasurable physical and mental diligence.
They deeply give rise to great vows,
practice great skillful means,
and manifest great compassion.
One seeks great wisdom, up to and including the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head;
one seeks such great dharmas of all Buddhas as these.
One should know that this is because the Dharma is immeasurable.
The retribution of merit and virtue is likewise immeasurable.

Next, regarding the "Gate of Encouraging the Superior and Inferior, the Weighty and Extensive," it is said that the superiority and inferiority of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) shall now be explained.
The Tathāgata has said:
"The meritorious fruit and retribution of even a single inferior thought of initial resolve by a bodhisattva cannot be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
How much more so, then, could one ever fully describe the fruits of merit resulting from all the various states of mind cultivated over a single day, a month, a year, or even a hundred years?
Why is this? Because the conduct of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible;
they desire to cause all sentient beings to abide in the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because they attain unsurpassed bodhi,
it is next illustrated by means of a simile to show its excellence:
"O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas first resolve upon bodhicitta..."
For example, when the great ocean first begins to arise,
one should know that it serves as the dwelling place for all kinds of wish-fulfilling jewels— those of inferior, middling, and superior value, even up to those of priceless value.
Because these jewels are all produced from the great ocean,
so too is the bodhisattva’s production of the mind of awakening:
it is the source from which the meditative concentrations, wisdom, and all merits of those of the three vehicles arise.
Furthermore, it is like when the trichiliocosm first begins to arise;
one should know that this serves as [the basis] for all sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of existence.
They all bear [the burden] and serve as a place of reliance;
the Bodhisattva is likewise when first gradually arising.
Universally for all immeasurable sentient beings—
namely those of the six realms and four modes of birth,
whether possessing right view or wrong view.
Cultivating good and practicing evil;
observing the precepts and violating them;
revering and honoring the Triple Gem.
They slander and revile the True Dharma,
as well as all Māras, non-Buddhists,
śramaṇas, and brahmins.
Extending even to the four castes,
it serves as a support for all who bear their burdens;
next is the characteristic of the awakening that arises from the initial resolve.
Taking great compassion as the foundation,
I shall now explain how bodhisattvas cultivate compassion and so forth,
providing a detailed exposition on the objects and modes of cultivation for loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The objects of perception are explained through analogies,
such as the dust motes of the great earth, the waters of the great oceans, a single trichiliocosm, and even the immeasurable limits of the ten directions;
since the realms produced by these objects of cognition are vast and inexhaustible.
The bodhisattvas’ resolve is able to completely cover all such sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha,
how could this bodhicitta ever be exhausted?
If there is a bodhisattva who,
upon hearing such an exposition,
is neither startled nor terrified.
They do not fall back and do not sink;
one should know that such persons are certain to be able to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Even if there were immeasurable Buddhas, Tathāgatas...
Even if one were to praise their merits for immeasurable eons,
they could never be exhausted. Why is this?
Because the bodhicitta is boundless and impartial,
it next explains the causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta, saying:
"If bodhisattvas draw near to spiritual friends..."
Making offerings to all Buddhas,
cultivating and accumulating roots of goodness,
and aspiring to seek the supreme Dharma.
The mind is always gentle and supple;
one is able to endure suffering when encountered;
and compassion is profound and sincere.
With a profound mind of equanimity,
they have faith in and delight in the Mahāyāna,
seeking the wisdom of the Buddha.
If a person can possess these ten dharmas,
they are then able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there are eight ways to draw near to virtuous friends.
The ninth verse of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"Tranquil, disciplined, and possessing the virtue of elimination;
courageous and rich in scriptural knowledge."
"Awakened, he truly and well expounds the Dharma;
his compassion is profound and free from decline.
This verse clarifies the first reliance: intimate association.
A virtuous friend who is endowed with ten kinds of merit should be worthy of being relied upon. What are these ten?
First is subduing,
which means being in accordance with the precepts,
due to the subduing of the faculties.
Second is tranquility,
which refers to being associated with meditative concentration due to internal withdrawal.
The three delusions are eliminated;
that is to say, faith, mindfulness, and wisdom are associated [with the path],
because the afflictions have been severed.
Fourth, the increase of the four virtues,
meaning that precepts, concentration, and wisdom are complete and without deficiency.
Fifth, possessing courage.
That is to say, it is because one does not grow weary when benefiting others.
Sixth is wealth of scripture,
which means having attained great learning.
Seventh is being true,
meaning that one realizes the actual meaning.
Eighth is being well-spoken.
Because it is non-perverted;
ninth, its compassion is profound because it is free from expectations.
Tenth, the absence of regression.
Because one speaks with reverence at all times, this is the characteristic of a virtuous friend whom one should approach.
Second, there are three ways of approaching through material things.
First, material wealth,
which refers to respectful offerings;
second, the person.
This refers to serving in accordance [with the preceptor].
It consists of three aspects of mind: that is, when serving, the body and mind are in harmony.
Regarding the third condition, approaching virtuous friends, there are three aspects:
first, aspiration and delight;
second, knowing the proper time.
Third, the removal of pride;
fourth, dedication and cultivation of intimacy,
without being attached to gain or offerings.
However, for the sake of practicing in accordance [with the teachings],
one approaches through five causes.
Approaching by practicing in accordance with the instructions received is the cause of approach.
Why is this? Because by acting in accordance with this,
one causes that virtuous friend’s mind to give rise to joy.
Sixth is the cultivation of the six types of knowledge,
in order to skillfully understand the three vehicles and bring one's own vehicle to fulfillment.
Seventh is the cultivation of a spiritual friend as a field of merit.
That is to say, it refers to the adornment and purification of the buddha-field. What is meant by "field"?
It is that which one has heard of the Dharma oneself.
Because it is established within the mental continuums of sentient beings;
because it cultivates the causes for purification according to the buddha-field in which one dwells.
Eighth, regarding reliance and cultivation:
One relies solely on the fulfillment of the benefit of the Dharma;
therefore, one draws near to virtuous friends.
One does not rely on the fulfillment of material gain.
There are six distinctions regarding the cultivation of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
First is the distinction of cause and effect:
that is, past cultivation serves as the cause.
The present is the fruit;
the present is the cause;
the future is the fruit.
Second is the differentiation according to the Dharma:
this refers to practicing in accordance with the specific distinctions of the Dharma-gates taught by spiritual friends.
Third is the distinction between internal and external:
approaching [the practice] oneself is internal;
causing others to approach it is external.
Fourth is the distinction between the coarse and the subtle:
listening for oneself is coarse;
internal mental reflection is subtle.
Fifth, the distinction between superiority and inferiority:
approaching with pride is inferior;
approaching without pride is superior.
Sixth is the distinction between near and far.
Rebirth in the present life is near;
rebirth in the next life (upapadyavedanīya) is far.
Birth-retribution, subsequent retribution, and uninterrupted retribution correspond respectively to near and distant lifetimes.
What are the five types of supreme attendance?
First, pure faith.
Because one gives rise to pure faith toward those with whom one associates.
Second, the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*);
herein there are nine [types].
First, the mind of single flavor;
second, the mind of sympathetic joy;
third, the mind of aspiration.
Fourth, the mind of insatiability;
fifth, the vast mind;
sixth, the mind of supreme joy.
7. The mind of victory;
8. The undefiled mind;
9. The well-purified mind.
The three supernormal powers (abhijñā).
This refers to approaching them by relying on samādhis such as the Ākāśagarbha-samādhi.
The four skillful means refer to being subsumed by non-conceptual wisdom.
As for the fifth, "concordance":
This means that because a great bodhisattva enters all fruits by means of a single fruit, each of those ten types of practice should be explained.
Furthermore, there are four conditions:
first, the contemplation of all Buddhas.
There are five further ways of generating the bodhicitta: first,
reflecting upon all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
At the initial moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, one possesses the nature of afflictions, just as I do now; yet,
in the end, one will attain perfect awakening.
One becomes the Unsurpassed Honored One.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta.
Second, by contemplating all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one gives rise to great courage and vigor.
Each and every one of them is able to attain unsurpassed bodhi.
If this bodhi were a dharma that could be attained,
then I too should have attained it.
For this reason, thirdly,
one contemplates that the Buddhas of the three periods of time have given rise to great luminous wisdom,
establishing a supreme mind within the shell of ignorance.
Those who accumulated ascetic practices were all able to extricate themselves and transcend the triple world; I,
too, shall likewise extricate and rescue myself.
For this reason, fourth,
one should contemplate that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are heroes among men,
all of whom have crossed over the great ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions.
"I am also a great man and shall likewise be able to cross over.
For this reason, fifth,
one contemplates the Buddhas of the three periods of time and arouses great diligence.
Having sacrificed body, life, and wealth to seek all-knowledge,
I shall now likewise follow and learn from the Buddhas;
it is for this reason that I do so.
Observing the faults and afflictions of the body,
one gives rise to the bodhicitta;
furthermore, there are five kinds [of this].
First, one observes for oneself that the five aggregates and four great elements of one’s own body are all capable of producing immeasurable evil karma;
thus, one desires to abandon and leave them behind.
Second, one observes for oneself that the nine orifices of one’s own body constantly flow with foul, filthy, and impure substances.
Third, because one generates a sense of weary detachment;
that is, observing for oneself that one’s own body is ablaze with immeasurable afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, which burn the wholesome mind,
and wishing to extinguish and eliminate them.
Fourth, one observes for oneself that one’s own body is like a bubble or foam, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, and is thus a phenomenon to be abandoned;
this is because one wishes to cast it off.
Fifth, one observes for oneself that one’s own body is shrouded by ignorance, constantly creating evil karma and transmigrating through the five destinies.
Because there is no other benefit,
one seeks the most supreme fruit and resolves to attain bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are five matters.
First, seeing all Tathāgatas adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, their radiance pure and penetrating, which removes the afflictions of those who encounter them;
this is for the sake of cultivating and accumulating [these qualities].
Second, seeing that the *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas is eternally abiding, pure, and unstained,
for the sake of its cultivation and accumulation. Third,
seeing that all Tathāgatas possess the pure assemblage of the Dharma consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Fourth, because of the desire to cultivate and accumulate [these qualities], one perceives that all Tathāgatas possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness,
for the sake of cultivating and accumulating them.
Fifth, one perceives that all Tathāgatas possess omniscience;
they compassionately pity sentient beings, their loving-kindness and compassion universally covering them,
and they are able to lead all who are ignorant and deluded back to the right path.
For the sake of cultivation and accumulation,
one develops the bodhicitta out of compassion for sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, seeing that all sentient beings are entangled by ignorance;
second, seeing that all sentient beings are entangled by manifold sufferings.
Third, seeing all sentient beings accumulate unwholesome karma;
fourth, seeing all sentient beings commit extremely grave evils;
fifth, seeing all sentient beings fail to cultivate the true Dharma and being entangled by ignorance.
Furthermore, there are four matters:
first, seeing that sentient beings are deluded by ignorance and craving and thereby undergo great and intense suffering;
second, seeing that sentient beings do not believe in cause and effect and thus commit evil deeds.
Third, he saw that sentient beings had abandoned the true Dharma and accepted false teachings.
Fourth, he saw that sentient beings were submerged in the river of afflictions,
drifting on the four currents and entangled by manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, there are four matters.
First, seeing that sentient beings fear birth, old age, sickness, and death,
yet do not seek liberation and instead continue to create karma.
Second, he sees that all sentient beings are constantly creating suffering through grief and lamentation without ever ceasing.
Third, he sees that all sentient beings suffer from the pain of separation from those they love, yet fail to awaken to this and remain defiled by attachment to expedient means.

Fourth, seeing that sentient beings constantly give rise to resentment and jealousy due to the suffering of encountering those they hate, and further commit evil deeds, thereby accumulating unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, there are four other matters:
first, seeing that sentient beings commit various evils for the sake of sensual desire.
Second, seeing that sentient beings know desire gives rise to suffering yet do not abandon it;
third, seeing that sentient beings, though seeking happiness, do not possess the feet of precepts;
fourth, seeing that sentient beings, though not delighting in suffering, do not cease creating it, even committing the most grievous evils.
Furthermore, there are four matters.
First, sentient beings violate the grave precepts;
though they feel anxiety and fear, they remain negligent.
Second, they observe sentient beings who commit extreme evils,
suffering the calamities of the five *ānantarya* karmas; being stubborn and perverse,
they shroud themselves and fail to give rise to shame or remorse.
Third, he sees sentient beings who slander and revile the Mahāyāna Vaipulya True Dharma,
being exclusively foolish and self-attached,
and thus giving rise to arrogance. Fourth, he sees sentient beings who, despite possessing intelligence and wisdom, have severed their roots of goodness.
On the contrary, they are conceited and never repent or reform;
they do not cultivate the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four matters [regarding this].
First, he sees sentient beings born into the eight difficult conditions, where they do not hear the True Dharma and do not know how to cultivate goodness.
Second, he sees sentient beings who encounter a Buddha appearing in the world and hear the preaching of the True Dharma, yet are unable to receive and uphold it.
Third, he sees sentient beings who, having been defiled by the practices of non-Buddhist paths, undergo ascetic mortification of the body in their cultivation of karma, never attaining liberation.
Fourth, he sees sentient beings who cultivate and attain the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, yet claim it to be nirvana.
Once their wholesome retributions are exhausted, they fall back into the three miserable realms.
The Bodhisattva sees that sentient beings, through ignorance,
create karma and suffer for a long night.
They have abandoned the true Dharma and are迷失 (deluded) regarding the path of escape; it is for the sake of such as these.
He gave rise to great compassion and resolved to seek bodhi with the urgency of one whose hair or head were on fire.
For all sentient beings who possess suffering and affliction,
I shall deliver them so that none remain.
O Sons of the Buddha, I have now briefly explained the arousal of the mind through the causal conditions of a bodhisattva’s initial practice.
The Gate of Making Vows and Taking Oaths: Making vows and taking oaths.
How does a bodhisattva set out for enlightenment?
By what karmic practices does one accomplish enlightenment?
A bodhisattva who has resolved upon awakening and dwells on the stage of Dry Wisdom should first firmly establish right vows to gather in all immeasurable sentient beings.
I seek unsurpassed bodhi to rescue,
protect, deliver, and liberate all beings,
leaving none remaining.
They cause all beings to ultimately attain nirvana without remainder.
For this reason, at the very inception of generating the mind [of enlightenment], great compassion is foremost;
it is because of this compassionate mind.
One is able to give rise to ten further superior and supreme right vows. What are these ten?
First, may the roots of goodness planted by me in previous lives and in this present body [ripen].
I give all things away and dedicate them together toward unexcelled bodhi,
so that this vow of mine may increase in every thought-moment.
May it be never forgotten throughout successive births and be protected by dhāraṇīs.
Second, may I dedicate [this merit] toward great enlightenment.
By means of these roots of goodness,
may I always be able to make offerings to all Buddhas in every place of birth.
May there never be any buddha-fields where no Buddha is born.
Third, may I, having been born in all buddha-fields,
always be able to draw near to and attend upon [the Buddhas] at their left and right sides.
Like a shadow following a form,
may I never be separated from all Buddhas for even a single moment.
Fourth, may I attain proximity to the Buddhas.
He taught me the Dharma according to what was appropriate for me.

Again he asked:
"What is the basis of the wisdom of skillful means?

Again he asked:
"What is the basis of the mind of non-negligence?

Chapter on the Virtues of a Wife. **Chapter One: Praising the Reception of Precepts** The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle thirteen, states: [text follows]
If it is because of compassion for sentient beings,
because of the desire to deliver sentient beings,
and also because of knowing the true mark of the precepts.
The mind does not rely upon or cling [to anything].
Maintaining the precepts in this manner will cause one to attain the Way of the Buddha in the future.
This is called attaining the precepts of the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
If a person seeks the great benefit of goodness,
they should firmly uphold the precepts as if cherishing precious treasures.
One should protect it as one protects one's own life. Why?
It is like the great earth.
All things that possess form rely upon the earth to abide;
the precepts are likewise.
Precepts are the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas;
they are like one who wishes to walk but has no feet,
or one who wishes to fly but has no wings.
It is impossible for one who has no boat to desire to cross over; likewise,
it is impossible for one who does not maintain the precepts to desire to obtain good fruits.
It is likewise so. If a person abandons these precepts, even though they dwell in the mountains,
practice austerities, eat fruits, and take medicinal herbs, [they gain no merit].
They are no different from birds and beasts.
Although a person may be poor,
they can still maintain the precepts.
It is superior to worldly wealth and honor;
whereas the fragrance of one who has broken the precepts cannot be smelled from afar,
the fragrance of one who maintains the precepts pervades the ten directions.
One who upholds the precepts is endowed with perfect peace and happiness;
their fame spreads far and wide,
and they are cherished and respected by devas and humans alike.
In this present life, one will constantly obtain various forms of happiness.
Should one desire wealth, nobility, and long life among gods or humans,
these will be attained without difficulty.
Through the purity of upholding the precepts, all one's aspirations are fulfilled.
Furthermore, those who uphold the precepts are constantly honored and supported by people in this world;
their minds are joyful and free from regret.
They shall never lack food or clothing;
upon death, they shall be reborn in heaven,
and later attain the Way of the Buddha.
One who upholds the precepts shall not fail to attain anything;
one who breaks the precepts loses everything.
It is like a person who constantly makes offerings to a deity.
That person was poor,
yet he made offerings with single-minded devotion for a full twelve years.
When one seeks wealth and status, the heavens take pity on this person and manifest their own form to them, as explained in detail elsewhere.
Furthermore, regarding those who uphold the precepts, people delight in giving to them and do not begrudge their wealth or possessions.
Without cultivating worldly gain, one shall lack for nothing;
one shall attain rebirth in the heavens before the Buddhas of the ten directions,
enter the path of the Three Vehicles, and achieve liberation.
Those who maintain the precepts while harboring various wrong views will gain nothing in the end.
Furthermore, as for those who maintain the precepts:
Although they possess no weapons,
no manifold sufferings shall befall them;
for no one can rob them of the wealth of their precept-keeping.
Those who uphold the precepts remain inseparable from their kin even in death;
the adornment of upholding the precepts surpasses that of the seven treasures.
For this reason, [it is superior].
One should guard the precepts as one guards one's own life or as one cherishes a precious treasure;
for those who break the precepts undergo ten thousand forms of suffering.
It is like a poor person who breaks a jar and loses its contents;
for this reason, one should maintain pure precepts.

The Section on Revealing Faults. Furthermore, a person who upholds the precepts should observe the transgressions of those who break them and exert themselves to maintain the precepts with single-mindedness.
What are called the transgressions of those who break the precepts?
A person who breaks the precepts is not respected by others;
their home is like a tomb.
It is a place where no one can reach.
One who breaks the precepts loses all merit,
like a withered tree.
People do not love or delight in them;
those who break the precepts are like frost-bitten lotuses,
which people take no pleasure in seeing.
A person who breaks the precepts possesses an evil mind like that of a malevolent rākṣasa;
people do not turn toward one who has broken the precepts.
For example, a thirsty person does not turn toward a dry well; likewise,
the mind of one who has broken the precepts is constantly filled with doubt and regret,
just as a criminal is perpetually afraid that his punishment will arrive.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a field struck by hail;
one cannot rely upon them.
A person who has broken the precepts is, for example, like a bitter gourd.
Although its form resembles that of a sweet variety, it is inedible;
it is like a village of bandits.
One should not rely upon them;
they are like a person with a grave illness,
whom others do not wish to approach.
It is like a wicked thief,
difficult to approach;
it is like a pit of fire.
The practitioner avoids it;
it is like a venomous snake that must not be touched,
or like the great ocean.
Like a wrecked ship;
like vomited food;
like a vicious horse among good horses.
They differ from virtuous people,
like a donkey among a herd of oxen;
a person who has broken the precepts stands out within a community of those who are diligent.
For example, a weakling among strong men;
though one who violates the precepts may resemble a bhikṣu,
he is like a corpse among sleeping people.
Therefore, the practitioner should single-mindedly and firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts.
Regarding the "Encouragement to Uphold" (勸持門), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:

What benefit is gained now by not killing living beings?

because I have not harmed them.
He, too, cannot harm me;
for this reason, I am without fear or dread.
Even one who delights in killing may attain the supreme rank of a human king.

One who upholds the precepts travels alone and wanders singly without fear or difficulty.
Furthermore, as for those who delight in killing:
All living beings are displeased to see him; yet,
if he does not take pleasure in killing,
all sentient beings will joyfully seek to rely upon him.

"I cherish my own life and love my own body;

If one kills a living being...

detested by others,
and feel regret at the time of death.

even if they emerge as humans,
they shall always be short-lived.

nor be censured by virtuous people,
nor envied by enemies;

Furthermore, taking life is the gravest among all sins. Why is this so?
When people face the urgency of death,
they do not begrudge even their most precious treasures;
they prioritize nothing but saving their own lives.
It is like a merchant who has entered the sea to gather treasures;
as he is about to emerge from the great ocean,
his ship is wrecked and his treasures lost, yet he rejoices within himself.
The crowd spoke in astonishment:
"You have lost your wealth and property,
yet you have escaped in the nude."
"What do you mean by saying that one loses a great treasure?
The answer is: among all treasures, human life is foremost.
It is for the sake of life that people seek treasures."
One does not seek life for the sake of wealth; for this reason,
among the Buddha’s ten unwholesome paths of action, killing is placed first.
If a person cultivates various kinds of merit and virtue but lacks the precept against killing,
it will be of no benefit.
Why is this? Although one may be born into a position of wealth and honor with great power and influence,
there is no such thing as a permanent life-span.
Because of who experiences this pleasure,
the sin of killing is grave;
among all virtues, non-killing is supreme.
Furthermore, among all things in the world, the cherishing of life is paramount. How is this known?
Because all people in the world willingly endure various forms of physical torture and interrogation.
This is for the sake of protecting one's life.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are five great gifts,
which are precisely the five precepts.
Furthermore, practicing the samādhi of loving-kindness brings immeasurable merit;
one cannot be harmed by water or fire.
They will not be harmed by blades or clubs,
nor can they be affected by any poisonous venom,
because of their five great acts of giving.
The results obtained are thus.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of offenses for taking life,
as the Buddha spoke to the upāsaka Nandika.
There are ten offenses in taking life. What are these ten?
First, the mind constantly harbors poison.
It continues without interruption from lifetime to lifetime.
Second, sentient beings harbor hatred and loathing;
they take no pleasure in seeing it with their eyes.
Third, they constantly harbor evil thoughts and contemplate wicked matters.
Fourth, sentient beings fear them as if seeing a snake.
Fifth, while sleeping, the mind is fearful,
and even upon waking, it remains uneasy.

Seventh, at the time of death, one undergoes a mad, terrified, and evil death.
Eighth, one plants the causes for a short life.
Ninth, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the hells.
Tenth: if one is reborn as a human being, one will always have a short lifespan.
[The opponent] asks: "If I do not harm you, may your intent to kill cease."

one should weigh the gravity of the matter.

"The benefit of preserving my precepts is weighty;
the benefit of preserving my life is weighty."
Violating the precepts is a loss;
losing one's body is a loss.
Having reflected thus:
One should know that upholding the precepts is of primary importance while preserving the body is secondary.
If one merely seeks to preserve the body,
what benefit will that body bring?
This body is called a thicket of old age and death;
it must inevitably perish.
Even if one loses this body for the sake of upholding the precepts, it is well.
The benefit thereof is exceedingly great.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"I have repeatedly lost my life in the past and present."
Throughout countless lifetimes, I have engaged only in unwholesome deeds for the sake of wealth and profit;
now, having attained the ability to uphold the pure precepts,
I shall not begrudge this body and will sacrifice my life to maintain them.

[the parents] provide the knife and a single sheep.
He confined him within the house and spoke to him, saying:

The sheep stood on one side.

There are ten offenses for taking what is not given. What are these ten?

third, acting at improper times without due deliberation;

Tenth: If one leaves [the religious life] to become a layperson and diligently seeks wealth, yet shares in the suffering of the five families and engages in sexual misconduct.
A question is asked:

the sentiment between husband and wife is such that they are different persons yet one body.

There is little joy and much fear;
one fears execution and punishment,

which is censured by the Noble Ones.
Furthermore, one reflects upon this.
My wife and the wives of others are equally women;
in their physical form and emotional nature, there is no difference between us.
Why, then, do I give rise to perverse delusions and follow after such deviant thoughts?
One who commits sexual misconduct destroys and loses the happiness of both this life and future lives.

If he violates my wife,
I shall become enraged; if I violate his,

The family life was not harmonious;
he constantly encountered lewd women,
and the afflictions of depravity, cruelty, and sexual misconduct plagued him.
It is like a venomous serpent,
and like a great conflagration;
if one does not avoid it with urgency, [it will cause harm].
Calamity is about to arrive,
