On the following day, he again spread new flowers over the previous flowers and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times.
He continued in this manner for up to seven days.
If one digs, water will immediately be found.
If there is much disease in the land,
one should grind the flower with cold water.
By anointing conch shells, drums, and other instruments,
or by blowing and striking them so that they produce sound,
those who hear it are immediately healed.
If an enemy state or a hostile kinsman intends to invade the borders,
one should take water and rub it with flowers, then sprinkle them in that location.
They will immediately be dispersed and driven away. If there is a flat rock on a high mountain,
many bhikṣus may rub flowers upon that stone.
When the offering of the *māndārava* flowers was completed, they prostrated together.
After a long time, precious jewels spontaneously grew upon the stone.
If a person is foolish...
Take the flowers offered, numbering as many as one hundred varieties down to seven,
and pound them into a powder.
First, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over ghee from a tawny cow.
Mix these together to form a pill the size of a small pellet.
Take one pill daily;
when taking the pill, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Gradually he attained intelligence and sharp faculties;
within a single day, he was able to recite a hundred verses.
If anyone has anything to do...
One should first make offerings of various flowers, such as the utpala, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and utpala, whether they grow in water or on land;
there are one hundred kinds of such flowers.
Afterward, one may moisten the flowers with water;
according to whatever is required— whether for anointing or scattering—
all shall yield their fruit.
If one obtains a hundred kinds of flowers,
grind them to create a powder;
mix with water to form pills.
If one rubs it upon a malignant swelling,
that ailment will be immediately cured;
whether it be an abscess, a carbuncle, or any kind of venomous poison.
Whether one ingests this pill or applies it to the skin,
the illness shall be immediately eliminated.
If a person constantly suffers from a depletion of their physical constitution due to foul odors,
by rubbing the juice of large or small barley onto flowers and applying them to the body,
they will immediately become refreshed and satisfied.
Furthermore, by mixing flower juice with unopened flowers to form pills and applying them to one's forehead,
all enemies will see one and give rise to feelings of affection.

Mañjuśrī, this flower-dhāraṇī rite is as follows: 1. *Namo buddhāya svāhā*. 2. *Namaḥ prajñāpāramitāyai svāhā*. 3. *Namo bhadracittāya svāhā*. 4. *Namo bodhiparigrahāya svāhā*. 5. *Namo dharmacakrāya svāhā*. 6. *Namo tathāgatāya svāhā*. 7. *Namo bodhisattvāya svāhā*. 8. *Namo saṃghāya svāhā*. 9. *Namo pāramitāyai svāhā*. Recite each mantra one hundred and eight times.
"You should recite these mantra verses in various places.
Just as it is with the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* Dharma, so it is with other dharmas.
Regarding the gates of obstacles and their remedies, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 79, states:
Briefly stated, there are four superior obstructions for bodhisattvas;
if these are not thoroughly purified,
they will ultimately be incapable of entering the bodhisattva stages or the gradual progression through those stages.
What are the four? First, one incurs an afflicted transgression within the vinaya of the bodhisattvas.
Second, slandering the sublime Dharma associated with the Mahāyāna;
third, not having accumulated roots of goodness;
fourth, possessing a mind of defiled attachment.
To remedy these four, first,
one should, before all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions,
deeply and earnestly reproach oneself, confessing and repenting of one's transgressions.
Second, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
one exhorts and entreats all Tathāgatas to teach the Dharma.
Third, regarding all the merits possessed by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions...
Fourth, all roots of goodness that arise are entirely dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi. All rejoice in accordance with this.
Regarding the section on superiority and inferiority, the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, fascicle two,
states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five qualities that surpass the ten paths of wholesome action of the śrāvakas."
First, practicing with single-minded concentration,
because one never departs from the mind of a single flavor;
second, practicing constantly.
Because it is uninterrupted, unceasing, and without rest.
Third, it is for the sake of stabilizing one’s own person;
that is, to take on a human or celestial body for oneself.
It is for the sake of attaining the peace and security of the human and celestial realms as well as great enlightenment. Fourth,
it is for the sake of bringing peace and security to the bodies of others, by ultimately dedicating [merit] toward great enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings.
There are five kinds of wholesome purity.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, because it is unbroken.
Partial cultivation and refinement is called "breaking";
complete cultivation and refinement is called "not breaking.
These two are untainted.
Not practicing oneself but teaching others to practice is therefore called "illumination."
The Bodhisattva practices this himself and teaches others to practice it;
therefore, it is called "untainted.
Third is "unstained."
Because one does not practice oneself nor teaches others to practice,
yet feels sympathetic joy upon seeing others practicing,
it is called "defiled."
Therefore, the bodhisattva who fully practices this is called "unstained.
These four are without dependence;
one must rely on the wisdom of others in order to practice them.
Therefore, it is called "belonging.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva is able to practice without relying on the wisdom of others, it is called "being without belonging.
This is the fifth perfection of goodness.
Single-mindedly contemplating the ultimate cessation of desire and so forth is called "wholesome culmination.
This is the sixth non-eating [practice].
Because it is dedicated toward existence and grasps the requisites for existence,
it is called "nutriment."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva does not grasp at names, it is called "not eating.
This is praised by the seven types of wise ones;
they abandon the two vehicles and dedicate [their merit] toward the world.
To abandon the Mahāyāna and turn toward the Hīnayāna is what the wise do not praise. Therefore,
a bodhisattva does not turn toward the world from within the two vehicles.
It should be understood that within the Mahāyāna, not dedicating [merit] toward the two vehicles is what is praised by the wise.
Bodhisattvas have five qualities by which,
practicing the ten paths of wholesome action,
they are able to transcend the world.
First is the vow:
from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening,
the bodhisattva constantly serves as a field of merit for all the devas and humans of the world.
First, it is because they surpass those of the two vehicles. Second, it is security:
although the bodhisattva’s practice may be oppressed by the extreme sufferings of the world, [it remains secure].
Not abandoning bodhicitta,
because one practices with single-minded devotion;
this is the third, the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
Because they practice with the most excellent mind;
because all bodhisattvas practice the ten wholesome paths of action with the deepest affection;
thus, the four virtues are pure.
Because the Bodhisattva possesses three kinds of pure conduct regarding the ten paths of wholesome action,
what are the five skillful means?
In what dharmas does the Bodhisattva [apply them]?
By what skillful means does one practice the ten wholesome actions?
Furthermore, there are five kinds of dharmas.
One practices the immeasurable paths of the ten wholesome actions. What are these five?
First, immeasurable lifetimes.
Because of practicing for immeasurable time,
there are two immeasurable wholesome dharmas;
because those wholesome dharmas are immeasurable.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to immeasurable paths of wholesome action,
accumulating all merits so that they may be brought forth for enjoyment.
Third, the contemplation of the immeasurables:
this is because one contemplates immeasurable sentient beings, rather than a limited number of sentient beings.
Fourth, the exhaustion of the immeasurables.
For example, it is like a householder whose wealth is immeasurable;
he is one of great renunciation and one of great compassion.
One who practices great compassion is a great caravan leader,
because of their pity for all sentient beings.
The practitioner who does not regress from the mind [of awakening] gives rise to such a thought.
I am able to bestow immeasurable and boundless peace and happiness upon all those sentient beings.
The bodhisattva likewise practices by abiding in a profound mind,
dwelling with a mind of peace and security for the sake of all sentient beings.
Arousing a mind of great diligence,
one should reflect thus:
"I shall teach and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering."
They establish all beings within the bliss of nirvāṇa;
therefore, the bodhisattva’s practice of the five immeasurable dedications is inexhaustible.
By means of ten inexhaustible and immeasurable [factors],
one practices the paths of wholesome action,
which are likewise immeasurable.
Because they rely on prior dedications that are immeasurable,
the fruits of all the wholesome paths of action cultivated by Bodhisattvas are likewise immeasurable.
It is named "Infinite Dedication.
Regarding the gate of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): as for the characteristics of a single spiritual friend, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, fascicle 44, states:
It should be known that a bodhisattva accomplishes eight factors that enable them to serve as a spiritual friend with all characteristics perfected.
The first is abiding in ethical discipline.
First, they are without breach or flaw regarding all forms of ethical discipline.
Second, they possess extensive learning and have achieved awakened wisdom.
Third is the possession of realization:
having attained any one of the superior virtues produced through cultivation,
one reaches access to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Fourth is compassion: being inwardly endowed with loving-kindness and mercy,
one is able to relinquish one's own abiding in happiness within the present life.
He is diligent and untiring in benefiting others.
Fifth is fearlessness:
when he proclaims the teachings of the true Dharma for others.
Sixth is forbearance: not losing mindfulness or eloquence due to fear,
and [enduring] various unwholesome actions such as others' derisive laughter, mockery, contemptuous speech, opposition, and other unpleasant words or paths of conduct.
They are able to endure all things.
Seventh, they are free from weariness,
and their strength is full and powerful.
He is able to engage in extensive analytical reflection and preach the Dharma amidst the assembly with speech free from hesitation or impediment.
The mind is free from weariness.
Eighth is skillful speech:
the faculty of speech is perfected and does not violate the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The words are clear and distinct;
this is the work of a virtuous friend.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
If bodhisattvas possess five characteristics and are endowed with manifold virtues,
they are able to serve as spiritual friends.
What is done is not in vain.
First, one first desires to bring about benefit and happiness for others;
second, [one acts] toward that benefit and happiness.
Knowing things as they truly are,
possessing non-erroneous awakening;
third, regarding those skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
He teaches the Dharma in accordance with proper decorum,
adapting to what the assembly is capable of receiving;
he possesses the skill and power to perform the work of taming beings.
Fourth, the mind of benefiting others without weariness;
fifth, being fully endowed with impartial great compassion toward all sentient beings, whether inferior, middling, or superior.
The mind is without partiality.
If bodhisattvas accomplish five characteristics,
they cause the nature of a virtuous friend to become a basis for trust.
It causes others to hear from afar and give rise to supreme pure faith,
let alone seeing it with their own eyes;
first, it is sublime and wondrous.
His deportment was perfectly tranquil;
he was endowed with all the constituent parts [of a monk],
entirely free from agitation.
Second, being grave and dignified:
the three types of action manifest without agitation or disturbance.
Third, being free from hypocrisy.
Fourth, he is free from envy; he never gives rise to intolerance toward the gains, offerings, or respect received by others.
He does not intentionally feign a dignified and disciplined demeanor for the purpose of deceiving others.
They constantly request that he preach and subsequently encourage him to do so,
offering extensive respect with a heart free from flattery or deceit; yet,
upon seeing his preaching of the Dharma or his receiving of profit and honor, they [do not become envious].
They give rise to deep sympathetic joy,
as if they themselves had attained it.
Fifth is frugality.
With few possessions, they practice relinquishment as they arise. Through five kinds of characteristics,
the Bodhisattva acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) toward those beings to be converted.
First, the ability to admonish and censure;
second, the ability to cause one to remember;
third, the ability to provide instruction.
Fourth, they are able to provide instruction;
fifth, they are able to expound the Dharma.
It should be understood that a bodhisattva [acts] by means of these four characteristics.
Only then does one fully accomplish the close attendance upon a spiritual friend:
first, by serving the spiritual friend at all times, whether they are ill or healthy.
First, they constantly give rise to affection, respect,
and pure faith. Second, toward spiritual friends,
they offer respectful greetings and prostrations at the appropriate times.
They welcomed him with palms joined,
diligently cultivating the practice of harmony and respect as an act of worship.
Third, regarding spiritual friends,
one should provide them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness, as well as other articles for sustaining the body, in accordance with the Dharma,
making offerings at the appropriate times.
Fourth, regarding spiritual friends:
whether they are in harmony with or separated from the meaning of the Dharma, one should rely upon them correctly.
It functions according to mastery,
is without fluctuation,
and manifests reality as it truly is.
One should cultivate a mind of obedience to the teachings,
approaching [the teacher] at the appropriate times to respectfully serve, inquire, listen, and receive instruction.
According to the *Dharmapada-sūtra*,
at that time the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what constitutes a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?"
The Buddha said:
"A virtuous friend is one who skillfully understands the profound Dharma— emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing."

They thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are ultimately equal—devoid of karma and its retribution, devoid of cause and effect, their nature and characteristics being suchness (tathatā).
They abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Within ultimate emptiness, they establish [all things] with blazing intensity;
such are spiritual friends.
To illustrate this capacity through an analogy,
the *Dharmapada* states:
"O son of good family, a virtuous friend..."
These are your parents,
for they have nurtured you as the body of enlightenment.
A spiritual friend is...
These are your eyes;
because they guide you upon the path to enlightenment, the term "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) is omitted here for brevity. This should be understood accordingly.
These are your feet,
for they shall carry you away from birth and death;
these are your ladder.
It is for the purpose of supporting you all and leading you to the other shore;
it is your food and drink,
for it can cause your Dharma-body to increase.
This is your precious robe,
for it covers your bodies of merit;
this is your bridge.
Because it carries you across the ocean of existence,
it is your wealth and treasure;
because it thoroughly gathers you in and frees you from the suffering of poverty, it is yours.
These are your sun and moon,
for they illuminate you so that you may be free from darkness;
these are your life-force.
Because it protects and cherishes you so that there is no time of fear,
this is your armor and staff;
because it subdues all māras and attains fearlessness.
This is your rope,
for it shall pull you out and lead you away from hell;
this is your sublime medicine.
It is for the purpose of treating the disease of your afflictions;
it is your sharp sword,
for it cuts through the net of all your cravings.
This is your rain,
for it moistens the sprouts of your enlightenment;
this is your lamp-light.
Because it can shatter the darkness of your five hindrances,
it is your excellent banner;
because it instructs you on how to proceed toward the right path, it is your guide.
This is your firewood and fire,
for it ripens the food of nirvana for you all;
this is your bow and arrow.
Because he shoots and slays the thieves of your afflictions,
he is your heroic general;
because he is able to shatter the army of your birth and death, he is your hero.
This is your Tathāgata,
for he destroys your afflictions and leads you to nirvāṇa.
Noble son, such is a spiritual friend.
There are such immeasurable merits as these;
therefore, I now instruct you to draw near to them.
Then, Bao-ming and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha speak this sublime Dharma and these essential phrases regarding spiritual friends, [were filled with joy].
They raised their voices and wailed,
tears falling like rain;
they wept with sorrow and were filled with anguish.
Unable to take his own life,
he thought to himself:
"My body has come from kalpas as vast as space."
Being protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra),
they have today encountered the Tathāgata and are able to hear the profound Dharma.
To have encountered such [a person] is due to the power of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
it is not through my own power that this is possible.
I thought to myself:
"From the very beginning, we have never repaid our debt of gratitude nor have we approached [the Buddha] through skillful means."
Having spoken these words,
he raised his voice once more:
"The Great Text of Knowledge is identical to the Yoga."
The *Śīkṣānanda-vatsa-ṣaḍ-abhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra* states:
There are four types of evil associates (*pāpamitra*).
The first is one who harbors a heart of enmity within.
Externally, they feign intimacy as a form of acquaintance.
Second, they delight in speaking pleasant words in the presence of others,
yet speak ill of them behind their backs.
Third, when in a state of urgency,
one is anxious and sorrowful in the presence of others,
yet feels joy behind their backs.
Fourth, those who outwardly appear as close friends while inwardly hatching schemes of enmity.
There are likewise four types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
First, to appear outwardly like an enemy while harboring deep affection within;
second, to offer direct admonition in the presence of others.
Third, when others are ill or emaciated,
or when they face distress due to official requisitions or legal troubles, one relieves them of their anxieties.
Fourth, when seeing those who are poor or lowly, one does not abandon them.
One should constantly contemplate seeking skillful means to delight others in wealth.
Furthermore, there are four types of evil associates:
the first are those who are difficult to admonish, instruct, or teach to do good.
Therefore, he associates with those who are evil.
Second, he is taught not to take as companions those who delight in wine;
therefore, he associates with those who are addicted to drink.
Third, as for the self-preservation of the teachings,
there are even more matters to attend to.
Fourth, the teachings should form friendships with the worthy.
Therefore, he was on intimate terms with Bo Yanzi.
Furthermore, there are four types of virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The first is one who, upon seeing a person in poverty, [acts accordingly].
First, base it on the ordinances to bring about order.
Second, do not engage in disputes or contentious calculations with others.
Third, go there daily to observe and report on the situation.
Fourth, one should always maintain mindfulness of one another while sitting or rising.
Furthermore, there are four types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*):
the first is one who has been arrested by officials.
He intended to hide it away and resolve the matter later; however,
both of them became ill and emaciated.
When returning to care for them, one views them as such;
when their acquaintances have died, one views them through the process of encoffining and interment.
Fourth, after a spiritual friend has passed away, one continues to keep their household in mind.
Furthermore, there are four types of spiritual friends:
the first is one who stops a quarrel when it is about to break out.
Second, when wishing to follow evil associates,
one should admonish and stop them.
Third, one does not wish to seek a livelihood through worldly means.
First, they encourage them to engage in productive livelihoods.
Second, they teach those who take no pleasure in the Way of the Sūtras so that they may come to believe in and rejoice in it.
Furthermore, there are four types of evil associates.
The first is one who becomes greatly enraged when others slight them even slightly.
Second, when a time of emergency arises,
he requests that someone act but refuses to go.
Third, when he sees another person in a state of emergency...
Fourth, seeing people die,
one abandons them and does not look upon them.
The Buddha said:
"Select those that are good and follow them;
distance yourself from those that are evil."
Because I followed along with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), I have personally attained Buddhahood.
Regarding the gate of mixed practices: the practice of a child serving their parents involves five matters.
First, one should mindfully attend to the management of one's livelihood;
second, one should rise early and instruct the servants and slaves to prepare meals at the proper time;
third, one should not increase the anxieties of one's parents.
Fourth, one should be mindful of the kindness of one's parents.
Fifth, when one's parents are ill or emaciated,
one should feel apprehension and seek out a physician to treat them.
Parents have five duties toward their children:
first, they should teach them to abandon evil and pursue good;
second, they should teach them arithmetic and writing.
Third, one should teach them to uphold the sutras and precepts;
fourth, one should arrange for them to marry early;
fifth, one should give them whatever one possesses at home.
A disciple serving a teacher should observe five matters:
first, one should respect and praise them;
second, one should be mindful of their kindness.
Third, one follows whatever has been taught.
Fourth, one contemplates it without weariness.
Fifth, one shall praise it in the future.
The teacher’s instruction of disciples also consists of five matters:
first, one should cause them to learn quickly;
second, one should cause them to surpass other disciples.
Third, he wishes to ensure that [the disciples] understand and do not forget;
fourth, he resolves all doubts and difficulties for them;
fifth, he wishes to cause the disciples' wisdom to surpass that of the teacher.
A wife has five duties toward her husband.
First, when the husband returns from outside,
she should rise to meet him.
Second, when your husband is away from home,
you must attend to the cooking, steaming, and cleaning while awaiting his return.
Third, you must not harbor lustful thoughts toward others outside the home.
If her husband reviles her,
she must not respond with words of anger.
Fourth, regarding all wealth and property, she must not hide or conceal anything according to her husband's instructions.
Only after five things have been brought to rest and stored away may one lie down to sleep.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which a husband should regard his wife:
first, he should treat his wife with respect whenever he enters or leaves.
Second, one should provide food, drink, clothing, and coverings;
third, one should provide gold, silver, pearls, and jewels;
fourth, one should entrust all that exists within the household, whether little or much, entirely to them.
Fifth, one must not harbor improper thoughts toward outsiders while maintaining attendants.
There are five matters concerning relatives and friends:
first, seeing them commit wrongful or evil deeds.
I shall admonish, enlighten, and restrain him in private.
Second, if there is any urgent distress,
I shall hasten to his aid for protection.
Third, one must not speak privately to others about what was said in confidence.
Fourth, one should mutually respect and praise one another.
One should divide whatever good things one possesses among them in proportionate shares.
A great man has five duties toward his slaves, servants, and laborers:
first, he must provide them with food, drink, clothing, and bedding at the proper times.
Second, if they fall ill or become emaciated, one should summon a physician to treat them.
Third, one must not strike or beat them recklessly.
Fourth, one must not confiscate their private property.
The five matters regarding property should be equitable.
There are also five matters concerning how a slave, servant, or handmaid should serve their master:
first, one should rise early by oneself and not wait to be called by the master.
Second, one should perform one's duties with a mind of self-reflection.
Third, one must cherish the master’s property and must not discard it or give it away to others.
Fourth, one should escort the master when entering or departing.
Fifth, one should later praise the Great Master's virtues and must not speak of his faults.
When serving a śramaṇa or a practitioner of the Way, one should employ these five matters.
First, direct a virtuous mind toward them;
second, choose kind words with which to speak;
third, show respect through your physical demeanor.
Fourth, one should feel loving admiration for them.
Fifth, śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way are heroes and teachers among men;
one should serve them with reverence and inquire about the ways of the world and the path to liberation.
A śramaṇa or practitioner of the Way should regard ordinary people with six intentions.
Teaching [them] from generosity up to wisdom constitutes these six.
The śramaṇa or practitioner of the Way teaches the abandonment of evil for the sake of goodness.
The kindness of revealing the true path is greater than that of one's parents.
Regarding the "Gate of the Conduct of a Wife," the *Yujie jing* (Sūtra of the Woman Yujie) states:
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"A woman ought not to rely on her own physical beauty to treat her husband with contempt.
What constitutes being 'handsome'?"
To eliminate eighty-four defilements of depraved states and to maintain a concentrated mind with single-minded focus—
this is what constitutes being upright and well-composed.
One does not consider a fair complexion, white hair, or dyed garments to be signs of virtue.
Within the bodies of women there are ten evil things. What are these ten?
First, when a woman is first born and falls to the ground,
her parents do not rejoice.
Second, in raising and nurturing her, they find no pleasure.
Third, the minds of women are constantly fearful of others.
Fourth, their parents are perpetually anxious regarding their marriage.
Fifth, they are separated from their parents during their lifetime.
Sixth, she was always apprehensive of her husband;
she watched his facial expression, and whenever he appeared joyful, she herself would immediately rejoice.
Seventh, she fears anger and resentment.
Eighth, it is extremely difficult for her to conceive and give birth.
Ninth, as a woman, she is frequently constrained and controlled by her parents.
Ninth, one is constrained by the prohibitions of being a son-in-law.
Tenth, in old age, one is rebuked by one's children and grandchildren.
From birth until death, one never attains autonomy.
These are the ten evils.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"In the service of her parents-in-law and husband by a wife, there are five virtues and three evils."
What are the five virtues?
First, as a wife, one should go to bed late and rise early;
one should comb and adorn one's hair.
Adjust your robes and wash your face and hands;
let there be no filth or impurity.
When undertaking any task,
first inform those who are honored;
one’s mind should always be respectful and compliant.
First, even if there is something sweet and delicious,
one must not eat it first.
Second, one must endure being scolded or reviled by one's husband.
One must not harbor anger or resentment.
Third, one must maintain a single mind in devotion to her husband and must not entertain thoughts of sexual misconduct.
Fourth, she should always wish for her husband’s long life.
Fifth, when the husband goes abroad on a journey,
the wife should properly attend to the household.
Constantly recollecting what is good and not recollecting what is evil—
these are the five virtues.
What are the three evils?
First, she does not serve her mother-in-law and husband with the propriety due to a wife;
she desires only fine food and takes it to eat first herself.
He goes to bed early before dusk and does not rise until after sunrise.
If his husband rebukes or instructs him, [he remains thus].
She glares at her husband with angry eyes and should reject him while scolding him alone;
second, she does not direct her whole heart toward her husband.
First, she thinks only of other men;
second, she desires her husband’s death so that she may remarry early;
third, she harbors such thoughts—these are the three evils.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"In the world there are further seven kinds of wives.
The first kind of wife is like a mother."
Second, like a younger sister;
third, like a spiritual friend;
fourth, like a wife.
Fifth, like a maidservant;
sixth, like an enemy;
seventh, like one who robs one of life.
A mother-in-law is one who loves and cherishes her son-in-law as if he were her own compassionate mother.
He attended him day and night,
never leaving his side,
and served him with all his heart.
One must not miss the proper timing.
For if one were to come and go [at inappropriate times],
I fear it would lead to being treated with contempt.
Upon seeing them, she felt compassion;
her heart never grew weary,
and she cherished her husband as if he were her own son.
As for the sister-in-law,
she serves her husband with the utmost reverence and sincerity;

Regarding the "Chapter on Attaining and Abandoning," the forty-second [chapter] of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
If a bodhisattva commits any one of the four dharmas of defeat (*pārājika*), [he loses his status].
How much more so for one who violates all [the precepts];
such a person will no longer be capable of increasing and gathering the vast provisions for bodhi within this present life,
nor will they be capable of purifying their intention within this present life.
Such a person is called a counterfeit bodhisattva,
not a true bodhisattva.
This applies if a bodhisattva employs a weak or middling degree of entanglement.
If one violates the four types of *pārājika* dharmas,
even though one does not relinquish the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
the violation through a superior grade of entanglement (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*) is termed "relinquishment."
If bodhisattvas repeatedly commit the four types of defeats (pārājika),
acting upon them again and again without any sense of shame or dread,
and developing a deep attachment to them;
Seeing these merits,
one should know that this is called an offense of the highest degree of entanglement;
it is not the case that all bodhisattvas who momentarily manifest a defeat constitute such an offense.
One then abandons the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
just as bhikṣus who commit an offense involving defeat immediately forfeit their prātimokṣa vows.
If a bodhisattva, through such a transgression,
abandons the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline,
they are capable of receiving it again within this very life.
It is not that they lack the capacity;
it is like a bhikṣu who, while abiding in the prātimokṣa vows,
commits an offense of defeat (pārājika).
In this present life, one is no longer capable of receiving [the vows] again.
Briefly stated, there are two conditions by which one relinquishes the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*):
first, the abandonment of the vow for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Second, by manifesting intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one commits an offense that constitutes a defeat (*parājika*).
Even if a bodhisattva were to take rebirth throughout the worlds of the ten directions, [they would still be considered to have fallen].
In whatever place they are born, they do not relinquish the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Because of this, the bodhisattva does not abandon the great vow for unsurpassed awakening,
nor do they manifest the commission of a defeat (*pārājika*) through the operation of intense fetters (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*).
If bodhisattvas, upon taking rebirth in another life,
should forget their original resolve,
they encounter virtuous friends who, desiring to awaken their mindfulness of the bodhisattva precepts, [act as their spiritual mentors].
Although it is experienced many times over,
it is not a new experience,
nor is it newly acquired.
It corresponds to seventy-five.
There are four conditions for relinquishing it:
first, the arousal of a mind that is discordant with the mind of undertaking the vow.
Second, before a discerning and noble person,
one intentionally utters words of renunciation;
third, one commits the four defeats (pārājika) either collectively or individually.
Fourth, by means of intense and superior entanglements (*paryavasthāna*),
they commit total or partial transgressions that accord with the four types of *pārājika* dharmas.
Furthermore, all such violations by this bodhisattva—
One should know that these are all subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
One should confess them before a person—whether of the Hīnayāna or Mahāyāna—who is powerful, capable of understanding the meaning of verbal expressions, and able to accept them.

If a bodhisattva commits an offense equivalent to the defeats (pārājika) as described above due to an intense fetter (adhimātra-paryavasthāna), they lose the ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara). They must confess and repent in order to extinguish [the offense].
One should undergo it again.
If one commits an offense against any of the aforementioned rules involving defeat due to a medium-grade entanglement,
one should do so before three individuals.
If the number exceeds this,
one should proceed according to the ritual for confessing and removing evil deeds.
First, one must state the name of the offense committed.
One should speak thus:
"Venerable One, please attend to me," or say, "Great Virtue."
I, [name], have thus transgressed the Dharma of the Bodhisattva Vinaya.
Regarding the matter as it has been confessed, I have committed an *āpatti* of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
The remainder is according to the procedure for confessing and extinguishing an *āpatti* of wrong-doing as practiced by a *bhikṣu*.
It should be stated thus:
if one commits an offense against any of the aforementioned *pārājika* rules or other offenses through a minor degree of obsession (*mṛdu-paryavasthāna*).
One should confess and repent before a single *pudgala*; this should be understood as being the same as previously described.
However, if there is no suitable *pudgala* before whom one may confess and eliminate the transgression committed, [one should proceed accordingly].
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with a profound and earnest intention, gives rise to a self-vow:
"I shall certainly guard myself against future transgressions so as never to commit them again.
In this way, one emerges from the offense and becomes pure once more.

The Method for Self-Administration of the Bodhisattva Precepts; Yoga, Chapter 41: Furthermore, when any bodhisattvas wish to receive the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), [they should proceed as follows].
If one does not encounter a person endowed with complete merit,
then at that time one should personally receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
One should receive it in this manner:
baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee upon the ground.
Or, squatting or kneeling,
they speak these words: "I,
named so-and-so, respectfully address all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages."
I now wish, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions,
to vow to receive all the training precepts of the Bodhisattvas and to vow to receive all the pure ethical discipline of the Bodhisattvas.
That is to say: the morality of restraint,
the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas,
and the morality of benefiting sentient beings.
Such training rules and such pure precepts have already been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past.
All bodhisattvas of the future shall fully possess them;
all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions now fully possess these points of training.
Regarding this pure precept:
all bodhisattvas of the past have already studied it;
all bodhisattvas of the future shall study it.
All present bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions are currently training in this;
the second and third [times] are also spoken in this same way.
Having finished speaking, one should rise.
All remaining points should be understood as previously explained by analogy with the "dharmas to be undertaken.
Regarding the gate of the eight victories and five perceptions: the gate of the eight victories and five perceptions first explains the characteristics of the excellence of practice.
First, the excellence of the path of single-minded pursuit; second, the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment;
third, the field of merit.
Fourth, possessing merit;
fifth, the lightness of retribution for committed offenses;
sixth, entering the womb.
Seventh, the supernormal powers;
eighth, the excellence of karmic fruition.
One gives rise to the five contemplative minds.
First, one should regard all sentient beings with the thought that they are like noble ones (*ārya*).
Second, one should regard them as like one's own parents.
Third, one should regard them as like one's teachers and elders.
The fourth is like the perception of a king;
the fifth is like the perception of a home.
Furthermore, one makes four vows.
First, all existing merits are shared equally with all sentient beings of the ten directions.
Second, one vows that all sentient beings of the ten directions shall cross over the ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions.
The third vow is that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may together master the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
with their words and meanings clearly understood.
The fourth vow is that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may together attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Ritual for Listening to the Dharma: Yoga Sūtra 44. When Bodhisattvas wish to listen to the Dharma, they should cultivate five types of perception while listening to the sublime Dharma from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
First, one forms the perception of it as a treasure,
because its meaning is difficult to obtain.
Second, one forms the perception of it as an eye.
Third, one forms the perception of light, because it serves as the causal nature for attaining vast, innate, and sublime wisdom.
Having already attained the vast, co-emergent eye of wisdom,
one knows all things as they truly are in every respect.
Fourth, one should form the perception of great fruit and supreme merit,
for it can lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa and the unsurpassed, wondrous state of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi).
Because it has the nature of being a cause,
one forms the perception of great, blameless joy in the present life.
Until one has attained nirvāṇa and perfect awakening (sambodhi),
one should discern phenomena as they truly are;
this is the faultless great bliss of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Because of the meaning of being the causal nature:
when bodhisattvas wish to hear the Dharma from a spiritual friend,
they [should regard] the Dharma teacher...
By means of five points,
one should not harbor divergent thoughts,
but maintain a purely sincere mind.
Listen attentively to the Dharma.
First, do not harbor divergent thoughts regarding the impairment of precepts;
that is, do not form the thought, "This is a violation of the precepts and a failure to abide in the code of discipline."
I should not listen to the Dharma from him.
Second, one does not harbor a prejudiced attitude toward those of ruined lineage;
that is, one does not think, "This person is of low birth."
I should not listen to the Dharma from him now.
Third, one should not harbor a contrary attitude toward the discolored appearance,
nor should one think, "This is ugly."
I should not listen to the Dharma from him now.
Fourth, one does not harbor divergent thoughts regarding the corruption of the phrasing;
that is, one does not think, "This person is not skilled at literary embellishment."
I should not listen to the Dharma from him now;
rather, I shall rely on the meaning and not on the letter.
Fifth, one should not harbor divergent thoughts regarding corrupt speech.
That is to say, one does not think: "These words are coarse and harsh, and he harbors much anger;
he does not proclaim the various dharmas with pleasant speech.
I should not listen to the Dharma from him now."
Yogācārabhūmi, Chapter 38:
How does one seek to hear the true Dharma?
It refers to when bodhisattvas, regarding well-spoken teachings...
One should abide in intense longing and reverence for seeking to hear the true Dharma.
To briefly describe the characteristics of intense longing and reverence:
it means that bodhisattvas, desiring to hear even a single well-spoken teaching, [exert themselves with such fervor].
Even if one’s path were to lead across a ground of blazing, fiercely burning iron,
and there were no other means by which one could hear this teacher of the well-spoken Dharma,
one would nonetheless give rise to intense love and reverence.
They enter with joy;
how much more so when they wish to hear many words of virtuous meaning!
Furthermore, regarding their own persons, the bodhisattvas—
And regarding all requisites for sustaining the body, such as food and drink,
whatever affection and esteem one previously had will not equal even one hundredth part of the affection and esteem one has now.
It does not even approach a fraction of an *upaniṣad*.
In this way, the bodhisattva conceives a heart of deep respect for well-spoken Dharma and constantly delights in hearing all well-spoken teachings.
They are free from weariness and lack no sense of satiety;
their pure faith is profound and deep,
and their nature is gentle and harmonious.
Their minds are upright and their views are upright,
because they cherish and revere virtue and because they cherish and revere the Dharma.
Dwelling with the Dharma Master,
one should have no mind of criticism or challenge,
but rather a mind of reverence.
Free from pride, one strives solely for the sake of seeking what is good,
rather than for the purpose of manifesting one's own virtues.
Desiring to establish the roots of goodness in oneself and others,
and not for the sake of gain or honor,
the bodhisattva is endowed with such virtues.
One should go to the place where the Dharma Master is with a mind free from defilement and a mind free from distraction.
Hearing the true Dharma.
What is meant by "an unstained mind"?
It refers to the time when one hears [the Dharma].
His mind is free from the defilement of arrogance,
free from the defilement of contempt,
and free from the defilement of cowardice.
One is free from the defilement of arrogance due to six characteristics;
that is to say, when listening to the Dharma,
one listens at the appropriate time.
Listen with earnestness;
listen with reverence;
do not harbor malice.
One does not comply with them and does not seek out their faults;
by means of these four characteristics, one is free from the defilement of disparagement.
When listening to the Dharma,
one should revere the sublime Dharma and revere the person who preaches the Dharma.
Do not disparage the true Dharma,
nor disparage the one who speaks it.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma:
One does not disparage oneself.
By this single characteristic, one remains free from the affliction of cowardice.
How does one listen to the sublime Dharma with an undistracted mind?
That is to say, by way of five aspects:
first, listening to the true Dharma with a mind seeking realization and understanding;
second, a mind that is single-pointed and focused.
Third, to listen with focused attention.
Fourth, to sweep away and purify the mind.
Fifth, to collect all mental states in order to hear the True Dharma.
For what reason do they seek the Dharma?
It is because when Bodhisattvas seek inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*),
it is for the sake of correctly practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
In order to provide extensive instruction for the benefit and awakening of others,
when seeking the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*),
one does so with the desire to understand, as they truly are, the faulty arguments found in the treatises on logic composed by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It is for the purpose of subduing the various heterodox arguments of others;
it is for the purpose of causing those who have not yet attained pure faith in this true, holy teaching to attain pure faith,
and for causing those who already possess pure faith to increase and expand it further.
When seeking the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*),
it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings who take pleasure in the classical language to develop deep reverence and faith toward the person of the Bodhisattva,
and for the purpose of awakening an entry into the distinctions among glosses, phonemes, and syntactic phrases.
Within a single meaning, he teaches through various categories and diverse sounds according to the occasion.
When seeking the science of medicine,
it is for the purpose of pacifying the various diseases of sentient beings.
Desiring to benefit the entire great assembly,
if bodhisattvas seek the vidyā of crafts and arts,
it is for the purpose of accumulating vast wealth with little effort.
It is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
it is to inspire in sentient beings a sense of profound wonder;
and it is by means of skillful wisdom to impartially distribute benefits, thereby aiding and gathering in immeasurable sentient beings.
One seeks these five sciences in order to swiftly bring to completion the great accumulation of wisdom for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the teaching of the Dharma, there are two ways in which a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma to others.
First, discourse that is conformable;
second, discourse that is pure.
Discourse that is conformable is as explained in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
One who speaks with purity should dwell in a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings who harbor enmity toward oneself and teach them the true Dharma; likewise,
one should do so toward those who engage in evil conduct.
Abiding in a mind of benefit,
one should preach the True Dharma to all sentient beings— those who lack happiness, those who suffer, those who are negligent, and those who are inferior.
One should abide in a mind of benefit, happiness, and compassion when preaching the true Dharma;
one must not, under the dominant influence of the fetter of envy, praise oneself and disparage others.
With a mind free from attachment,
one teaches the Dharma to others without hoping for gain, honor, or praise.
The Gate of Expedient Means for Gathering and Sustaining Beings: There are four kinds of expedient means that universally gather, discipline, and bring to maturity all sentient beings.
What are these four?
First, the skillful means of following and gathering;
second, the skillful means of being able to gather;
third, the skillful means of causing entry.
Fourth is the expedient means of conformity.
Practicing generosity is called the expedient means of conforming to gathering. Why is this?
First, one benefits sentient beings by means of various kinds of material wealth,
desiring to cause them to listen to and receive what is taught, and to practice according to those instructions.
If bodhisattvas subsequently practice kind speech,
wherever there are those who are deluded,
they do so with the desire to eliminate all that delusion so that nothing remains.
He causes them to embrace and examine correct principles.
Such kind speech is called the skillful means of embracing.
Once bodhisattvas know that those sentient beings have embraced and examined correct principles, [they proceed accordingly].
Next, one practices beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*):
uprooting those sentient beings from unwholesome states and exhorting,
training, settling, and establishing them in wholesome states.
This is called the skillful means of causing entry.
Once bodhisattvas have caused others to enter by such skillful means,
they finally engage in the practice together with them in the same correct activity.
He causes them to follow accordingly; by this means,
he ensures that those being converted do not make such a statement.
Since you yourself lack pure faith, ethical discipline, generosity, and wisdom,
how can you rely on them to exhort others, or to admonish, instruct, and reprimand them?
One provides reminders for them;
therefore, "common purpose" (samānārthatā) is called the expedient means of conformity.
Regarding the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, in the chapter on "Seeking the Dharma," there are four causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma.
First is form; second is non-form;
third is supernormal power.
The fourth is the True Dharma.
It is for the sake of form,
because it is the cause of the marks and signs of excellence.
It is non-material because it eliminates the causes of the afflictions;
it is supernormal power because...
Because it is the cause of mastery;
because it is for the sake of the True Dharma;
and because it is the inexhaustible cause.
As stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
a bodhisattva seeking the Dharma possesses four characteristics.
The first is the perception of it as a sublime jewel.
Because it has the sense of being difficult to obtain;
second, the perception of it as excellent medicine,
because it has the sense of removing illness.
Third, it is like the perception of wealth,
because its meaning is not dispersed.
Fourth, it is like the perception of nirvāṇa.
Because it has the meaning of the cessation of suffering,
one should regard the Dharma as being like a marvelous jewel, for it is the cause for the adornment of the marks and signs.
Because it is the cause for extinguishing the disease of afflictions, one should regard the Dharma as being like an excellent medicine.
Because the Dharma is the cause for mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is regarded as being like wealth;
because the Dharma is the cause for the inexhaustibility of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), it is regarded as being like *nirvāṇa*.
There are three kinds of greatness in seeking the Dharma.
First is the greatness of skillful means (*upāya-mahattva*),
because through supreme diligence one seeks the unerring reality of both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Second is the greatness of benefiting others (*parārtha-mahattva*).
He acts as the refuge for the world through the Dharma by establishing it in the ultimate truth; thus,
he possesses the greatness of self-benefit,
for he is fully satisfied with all virtues like the ocean.
The "Chapter on Entering the Monastery" in the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If a bodhisattva enters a monastery,
they should observe all the proper deportments and perform prostrations and offerings with reverence."
When householder bodhisattvas enter a Buddhist temple,
as they first approach the entrance,
they should prostrate themselves on the ground with their five limbs outside the temple gate.
One should think:
"This is the dwelling place of virtuous persons;
this is the dwelling place of those who practice emptiness."
The dwelling place of those who practice the signless;
the dwelling place of those who practice the wishless;
the dwelling place of those who practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
This is the dwelling place of those who practice right conduct and maintain right mindfulness.
If one sees various bhikṣus, one should observe their respective actions;
having seen them, one should remain reverent and respectful in heart.
When prostrating, attending upon, and inquiring after [the Buddha],
one should form this thought:
"Even if I were to do so for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges..."
He constantly performed great acts of giving at celestial shrines without ceasing;
yet he thought, "This is not as good as once going forth into the homeless life.
Furthermore, he reflected:
The household life is full of many faults and afflictions,
whereas the life of renunciation is free from them all;
this should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Reflecting on the merit obtained through the religious practices performed by those who have gone forth, [the bodhisattva thinks], "When shall I attain this?
He then extensively explains all the characteristics of the practices belonging to the three vehicles;
such is the bodhisattva at home who has already admired and aspired to the life of one who has gone forth.
When entering a stupa or monastery to pay homage to the Buddha,
one should give rise to three thoughts:
first, "When shall I attain such a state that I receive offerings from the eight classes of beings?"
Second, when shall I attain supernatural powers so that the relics may be distributed throughout the world to benefit sentient beings?
Third, with a profound mind, I now practice great diligence to attain great enlightenment.
After I have attained Buddhahood and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*,
I shall next go, according to my activities, to visit the various bhikṣus;
I shall invite those who understand the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) to the abode of the masters of discourse.
Regarding the questions on the observance and violation of the precepts, one should go to a Vinaya master;
regarding seated meditation and the practice of concentration, one should go to a Chan master, and so forth.
These are the gates through which one should protect the True Dharma. Because of five causes and conditions, a bodhisattva should receive and protect the True Dharma.
First, to know how to repay the kindness of all Buddhas;
second, to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time;
and third, to offer the most supreme offerings to all Buddhas.
Fourth, because it benefits immeasurable sentient beings;
fifth, because the True Dharma is most difficult to encounter.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga), fascicle 70:
Due to three faults, one is unable to listen to the sublime Dharma without error:
first, due to distraction;
second, due to delusion.
Third, because of a lack of respect.
There are five characteristics that constitute one who is a fit vessel for hearing and practicing [the Dharma]:
first, a humble mind.
2. The mind of practicing;
3. The mind of grasping the meaning;
4. The mind of skillfully grasping the meaning.
Fifth is the mind of reverence.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"One does not make noise during the six periods of the day."
When prostrating to the Buddha,
when listening to the Dharma,
and when the assembly is in harmony.
When eating, when taking formal meals,
and when defecating or urinating.
Why is this? Because that deity possesses a pure mind for the sake of hearing the Dharma,
and it is by means of that sound [that he does so].
Because their minds do not attain concentration,
the devas depart by means of their celestial power,
and malevolent spirits come to perform harmful deeds.
The Tenfold Classification of the Six Perfections. The seventh chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the "Chapter on the Compendium of the Perfections," states:
"In this context, the six pāramitās possess ten meanings."
First, the enumeration;
second, the manifestation of characteristics;
third, the sequence.
Fourth, the explanation of the names;
fifth, the cultivation;
sixth, the distinctions.
Seven, the practices of inclusion;
eight, the remedies for hindrances;
nine, the qualities.
The ten [aspects] mutually manifest.
First, the number six.
Furthermore, the first is explained as follows:
There are only six [factors] because they subsume three matters of self-benefit:
first, progress;
second, non-defilement.
First among the three non-perversions:
fourth, it causes the four matters to progress in their respective order;
first, the accomplishment of the necessities of life.
Through generosity,
one achieves perfection of the two [bodies]; through ethical discipline, one achieves perfection of the self.
Third is the accomplishment of retinue through patience;
fourth is the accomplishment of undertaking.
Because all undertakings are accomplished by means of diligence,
the fifth is meditative concentration.
Because it enables one to remain unstained by afflictions and to subdue them;
by virtue of this power,
the sixth is prajñā.
It ensures that karma is not inverted, because one knows all that is done as it truly is.
Furthermore, for the second reason, the number is exactly six in order to encompass the six matters of the two benefits.
First, it is to encompass the three matters of benefiting others.
In the preceding three instances, one should arouse right effort:
first, to give to others;
second, not to afflict others.
The three types of patience endure those afflictions;
they are placed last because they serve the three matters of one's own benefit.
First, they have their underlying causes.
By means of diligence, secondly, the mind abides;
for if the mind were not stable, it would not abide.
Third is liberation,
because once the mind is concentrated, it brings about liberation.
The third section further serves to encompass the six matters that benefit others.
Respectively, this is because it ensures that their enjoyments are not lacking,
because it does not cause them distress,
and because it endures their provocation.
To assist them in their endeavors so that they do not regress;
to cause them to turn toward [the path] by means of supernormal powers;
and to sever their doubts by means of skillfully expounding the Dharma.
Thus, benefiting others becomes the means to benefit oneself.
For the fourth reason, in order to encompass the four causes of the Mahāyāna, there are only six perfections.
The first is non-attachment (*asaṃkliṣṭa*).
Second, ultimate reverence;
third, non-retrogression;
fourth, non-discrimination.
When practicing generosity,
one is unstained by wealth because of the absence of attachment or longing.
When upholding the precepts,
one gives rise to the utmost reverence toward all points of training.
When practicing patience and diligence,
one does not regress from two things:
one endures the suffering inflicted by sentient beings and non-sentient beings.
Because one attains non-retrogression;
because one attains non-retrogression when progressing in the practice of virtue.
When practicing meditative concentration and wisdom,
these two are without discrimination,
because they are embraced in the equality of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Fifth, furthermore, it is for the sake of subsuming the six paths of the Mahāyāna.
What is the meaning of "path" (*mārga*)?
The answer is: that which possesses skillful means (*upāya*) is the path.
By means of giving,
one takes non-attachment to material resources as the path;
by means of ethical discipline, [one does so].
Not being distracted regarding objects is the path,
by virtue of patience;
not abandoning [beings] regarding birth is the path.
By means of diligence,
one causes those various virtues to increase as the path; by means of concentration,
[one achieves stability].
To take the purification of afflictions as the path is due to *prajñā*;
to take the purification of cognitive obstructions as the path is likewise due to *prajñā*.
Sixth, furthermore, there is an explanation of the three trainings based on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts.
Regarding the second point, the manifestation of characteristics, each possesses four aspects.
The first is the remediation of hindrances.
2. Wisdom; 3. Fulfilling vows; 4. Bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Regarding the "remedying of obstacles":

generosity (*dāna*) and the others remedy stinginess (*mātsarya*) and the other five hindrances respectively. Regarding the "integration with wisdom": [the six perfections are integrated with the six types of wisdom].
It proceeds together with non-conceptual wisdom because of the thorough realization of the selflessness of phenomena.
As for "fulfilling aspirations":
Regarding generosity, one bestows wealth upon those who seek it, providing whatever they desire.
Regarding ethical discipline, one protects them with body, speech, and mind when they seek precepts, and instructs them therein.
Regarding patience, one rejoices when others confess their transgressions.
In the case of undertaking activities, he assists according to their wishes;
in the case of meditative concentration, he bestows the Dharma according to their wishes;
and regarding doubts, he resolves them according to their wishes.
Regarding the maturing of sentient beings:
first, one gathers them through generosity;
subsequently, one brings them to maturity by means of the three vehicles, according to what is appropriate for each.
First, one establishes them within the precepts and so forth;
subsequently, their maturation through the three vehicles is likewise.
Regarding the third sequence, there are three causes and conditions.
First, preceding and succeeding;
second, lower and higher;
third, coarse and subtle.
Generosity is primary because it leads to subsequent qualities such as ethical discipline;
generosity is foundational.
Because it is superior to morality and the other perfections; giving is considered coarse,
while morality and the others are subtle.
All of these are to be understood in their proper sequence.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the name:
it is called "giving" (*dāna*) because it is able to eliminate poverty.
It is called "precept" because it can bring about coolness;
it is called "patience" because it can destroy anger and hatred;
it is called "diligence" because it can establish what is wholesome.
It is called concentration because it can sustain the mind;
it is called wisdom because it understands the true Dharma. Fifth is cultivation.
This is the same as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
and other treatises. Regarding the sixth distinction,
each possesses six meanings.
One intrinsic nature, one cause,
and three fruits.
Fourth, karma;
fifth, association;
sixth, categories.
As for its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it consists in giving one's own things to recipients.
As for its cause (*hetu*):
Because the wholesome root of non-attachment arises together with volition,
the fruit of giving consists in the accomplishment of both material wealth and one's own person.
Regarding "because of the accomplishment of the body," this subsumes the five [factors] beginning with life;
that is, one attains life.
One attains form,
attains power,
and attains bliss.
One attains discernment.
As for the agent of giving,
they encompass both self and others.
Regarding fulfillment and great enlightenment:
as for the correspondence with the fulfillment of giving,
it is because [the bodhisattva] dwells fully within the minds of those who are free from stinginess.
As for its categories:
it consists of the Dharma, wealth, and fearlessness.
As for its intrinsic nature:
Because one abides in the possession of the precepts and even masters the training in all the trainings.
As for the cause:
cessation is nirvana.
Because one undertakes and practices the precepts in order to seek nirvāṇa and cross over to the further shore of existence,
the fruits are rebirth in the happy realms, freedom from regret, and so forth.
One abides with a mind established in successive stages because it is attained through the precepts.
Regarding karma, there are three types.
First, it is able to sustain,
for it supports all meritorious qualities like the great earth.
Second, it is able to pacify all afflictions.
Third is fearlessness.
Because it cannot give rise to any causes and conditions for transgressions such as fear or hatred,
it is "associated."
Because at all times the actions of body, speech, and mind are exclusively virtuous.
As for its categories: it consists of two [types], one of which is obtained through a single reception.
One obtains both the *prātimokṣa* and the two dharmas [of meditative concentration].
One obtains the precepts of concentration and the path; the remaining details need not be recounted.
Check the text again.
Regarding the eight remedies:
because generosity (*dāna*) is free from the seven attachments,
the first is attachment to material wealth (*upakaraṇa*).
Second, attachment through negligence;
third, attachment through biased adherence;
fourth, attachment as a repayment of kindness.
Fifth, attachment to karmic retribution;
sixth, attachment to obstacles;
seventh, attachment to distraction.
Among these, attachment due to obstruction refers to the non-abandonment of the latent tendency of greed, which is the antithesis of generosity (*dāna*).
Attachment due to distraction is of two kinds.
First, distraction of mental application,
because of seeking the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Second, distraction of conceptualization.
Because of the discrimination of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*),
the remaining six obstacles and their remedies are the first five [remedies] which are the reverse of those [obstacles].
That is to say, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the abandonment of attachment to broken precepts, and so forth.
Regarding "precepts and so forth being free from attachment to obstacles":

this is because all latent tendencies (anuśaya) that constitute those obstacles have been severed. Regarding "precepts and so forth being free from attachment to conceptualization": [this is because they are free from the conceptual proliferation of grasping].
Because it does not differentiate among the three wheels.
As for the nine merits:
first, constant relinquishment.
This means that bodhisattvas, at all times, give their own bodies and lives to all who seek them;
second, they are free from seeking any reward for their kindness or any cherished fruit thereof.
Because great compassion is the cause,
one establishes the three types of bodhi:
through giving, one establishes the bodhi of the three vehicles for all sentient beings.
The four inexhaustibles are subsumed by non-conceptual wisdom and persist until even nirvāṇa.
That merit is inexhaustible,
providing endless benefit to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the six perfections possess pure merit.
Furthermore, those who beg from the Bodhisattva experience three kinds of joy:
first, the joy of seeing him.
Second is joy at the time when wishes are fulfilled.
Third is joy at the time of seeking to see and seeking fulfillment;
for joy does not arise when one does not see [the object] or when one's wishes are not fulfilled.
Because a bodhisattva experiences three types of joy in response to every supplicant, he likewise gives rise to three joys:
first, the joy arising at the time of seeing [the supplicant]; second, the joy arising when fulfilling their wish; [and third, the joy arising when they have departed].
Third, when seeking a vision [of the Buddha] and that seeking is fulfilled, one experiences joy.
In this regard, it should be understood that the three types of joy experienced by such seekers are not equal to those of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with great compassion,
the six perfections possess eight unsurpassed qualities.
The first is the basis.
Second, the two categories;
third, the three conditions;
fourth, the dedication.
Five causes,
six knowledges,
and seven fields.
The eight bases of reliance.
Regarding the basis of giving:
it is because one relies upon the bodhisattva.
There are three kinds: first,
giving material things,
because one relinquishes one's own life.
Second is the gift of fearlessness,
because it rescues and protects sentient beings who are suffering.
Third is the gift of the Dharma.
Because it explains the Mahāyāna Dharma;
as for the "condition," it is because great compassion serves as its causal condition (*pratyaya*).
"Dedication" refers to seeking great enlightenment;
"cause" refers to...
Because it takes as its cause the seeds of perfuming from the meritorious deeds of giving in previous lives;
and because the wise person observes the three spheres with non-conceptual wisdom.
There are five types of farmers:
first, those who seek others;
second, those who suffer.
Third, those without support;
fourth, those who practice evil;
fifth, those endowed with virtue.
Regarding the basis:
it is by virtue of three kinds of bases.
First, the basis of faith and inclination.
Second, reliance on reflection;
third, reliance on samādhi.
Seventh, the section on the seven gateways of apparent benefit; the twelfth, the adornment of the seven gateways of apparent benefit.
Bodhisattvas have seven kinds of semblances of benefit:
first, the semblance of a mother;
second, the semblance of a father.
Third, resembling a virtuous friend;
fourth, resembling a companion;
fifth, resembling a sturdy servant.
Sixth, resembling an ācārya;
seventh, resembling an upādhyāya;
and resembling a mother.
For example, a compassionate mother performs five acts of benefit for her child:
first, conceiving them in the womb;
second, giving birth to them.
Third, nurturing;
fourth, protection from harm;
fifth, instruction in speech.
The five activities by which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings are likewise:
first, directing a mind of equanimity toward sentient beings;
second, giving birth to them in the noble stages.
Third, nurturing all roots of goodness;
fourth, guarding against all misdeeds;
fifth, instructing and training through extensive learning.
For example, a compassionate father performs five kinds of beneficial deeds for his children:
first, sowing the seeds;
second, teaching them crafts and skills.
Third, to provide him with a wife;
fourth, to entrust him to virtuous friends;
fifth, to discharge his debts so that he need not repay them later.
The five activities of a bodhisattva are likewise:
first, causing faith to arise as the seed for the body of a noble one;
second, causing the training in higher ethics and concentration to increase as their craft.
Third, to cause them to obtain the joy and bliss of liberation as their marriage chamber;
fourth, to cause them to exhort and invite all Buddhas as their virtuous friends;
fifth, to eliminate all obstacles as the clearing of debts.
For example, a good friend performs five kinds of beneficial deeds for oneself:
first, concealing one's private words;
second, causing one to cease unwholesome conduct.
Third, praising virtuous conduct;
fourth, providing assistance in what is undertaken;
fifth, restraining the practice of evil deeds.
There are four kinds of evil deeds:
first, hunting;
second, sexual misconduct.
Third, indulgence in alcohol;
fourth, gambling.
The five activities of a bodhisattva are likewise.
First, one should keep profound teachings secret from those who are not suitable vessels;
second, one should reprimand those who violate the precepts in accordance with the Dharma;
third, one should praise those who possess the precepts with words of excellence.
Fourth, they instruct the practitioner so that they may swiftly realize [the goal].
Fifth, they cause one to become aware of demonic activities.
This is like having a wise companion who performs five kinds of beneficial services for oneself.
First, bestowing happiness;
second, bestowing benefit;
third, constantly bestowing happiness.
Fourth, they always bestow benefit;
fifth, they do not cause separation.
The five activities of a bodhisattva are likewise.
First, that which is non-erroneous worldly accomplishment is called "happiness" (*sukha*),
because by means of it one attains pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
Second, that which is non-erroneous supramundane accomplishment is called "benefit" (*artha*).
Because these serve as remedies for the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
the remaining three [applications of mindfulness] are easy to understand.
For example, it is like a capable servant who performs five kinds of beneficial services for his master.
First, one brings all activities to ultimate completion;
second, one becomes incapable of being deceived;
third, one endures all beatings and verbal abuse.
Fourth, their performance of tasks is excellent;
fifth, they are skillful in understanding expedient means.
The Bodhisattva is likewise.
First, maturing sentient beings;
second, revealing the essential path to liberation;
third, enduring all manner of evil deeds.
Fourth, bestowing worldly happiness;
fifth, bestowing supramundane benefit.
This is, for example, like a preceptor performing five acts of benefit for a disciple.
First, he instructs them in all dharmas;
second, he demonstrates the swift essentials;
third, his physical demeanor manifests a relaxed countenance.
Fourth, one knows how to speak with loving words.
Fifth, one has no expectations in the mind.
This is like a preceptor performing the five acts of benefit for his disciples.
First, he causes them to leave the household life;
second, he bestows the precepts upon them;
third, he restrains them from all transgressions.
The fourth is to sustain others with material wealth;
the fifth is to instruct them with the Dharma.
It is the same for a bodhisattva.
First, it causes the two accumulations to be fulfilled;
second, it causes liberation to be attained;
third, it causes all obstacles to be severed.
Fourth, bestowing worldly happiness;
fifth, bestowing supramundane benefit.
Regarding the five doors of aspiration for a bodhisattva: there are five points in which a bodhisattva constantly gives rise to aspiration.
First, the increase of the six perfections through aspiration;
second, the diminution of the six obscurations;
third, the maturation of sentient beings.
Fourth, the progressive advancement through the stages;
fifth, the aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment;
sixth, the gates of what must definitely be accomplished. Through the predominance of the six perfections, a bodhisattva attains six kinds of certainty.
First is the certainty of the accomplishment of wealth,
because through giving one constantly attains the accomplishment of great wealth.
Second is the certainty of birth in excellence.
Third is the certainty of non-retrogression through morality, because one always attains rebirth according to one's will;
and through patience, because one never retrogresses due to enduring all sufferings.
Fourth is the certainty of cultivation,
because one constantly practices virtue with uninterrupted continuity through diligence.
Fifth is the certainty of determinate karma.
Sixth is the certainty of effortlessness, because through meditative concentration one never regresses from the activity of maturing sentient beings,
and through wisdom one attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because non-conceptual wisdom abides spontaneously,
and in order for Bodhisattvas to accomplish the six perfections,
they must certainly perform six tasks within the various stages (*bhūmi*).
First, one must certainly make offerings;
second, one must certainly train in the precepts;
third, one must certainly cultivate compassion.
Fourth, one must certainly be diligent in the wholesome;
fifth, one must certainly distance oneself from clamor;
sixth, one must certainly delight in the Dharma.
In this sequence, one is able to fulfill the six pāramitās.
A bodhisattva must constantly perform six tasks:
first, to feel weary of the five desires.
First, because they do not cling to the karmic rewards of giving.
Second, they reflect upon their own faults,
meaning that throughout the six periods of day and night, they constantly examine the three types of action they have performed.
To know one's faults and reform them;
third, to endure suffering;
fourth, to cultivate goodness.
Fifth is "not relishing," which means not savoring the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rasa*),
because one constantly seeks rebirth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Sixth is non-discrimination.
This enables the six perfections (pāramitās) to be fulfilled in their respective order.
Regarding the ninefold doors of discrimination for the six perfections, see *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 39.
The perfection of giving has nine gates;
this applies likewise up to the perfection of wisdom.
As the verse says:
In nature, all difficulties are overcome;
through every gateway, one is a true person;
and in every way, all requests are fulfilled.
Happiness and purity in both worlds—
these nine aspects constitute a brief explanation of giving.
Regarding the first,
its intrinsic nature is the volition arising together with non-attachment, as well as that which is produced by its causes, capable of bestowing all things that ought to be given.
He is able to bestow all blameless objects of giving;
his two actions of body and speech are certain to bear fruit;
and seeing whatever is desired, he immediately practices generosity with those very things.
This is called the intrinsic nature of giving.
Second, regarding "giving everything," there are briefly two types.
First, objects of giving that are internal;
second, objects of giving that are external.
Giving only one's own body is called "internal object of giving."
If one gives out of compassion for sentient beings who subsist on vomit, giving them the food they have repeatedly eaten and then vomited,
it is called a "mixed gift of internal and external.
This excludes the types of giving described above.
