All other objects that ought to be given are called "merely external giving.
One should recognize that such internal and external giving merely brings comfort to those sentient beings, but does not bring them true benefit.
If it is neither beneficial nor conducive to well-being,
one does not give; conversely,
if it is the opposite, one gives.
There are extensively immeasurable instances of what ought to be given but was not given;
these may be understood by applying the same principle.
Third is the gift that is difficult to practice.
To possess meager wealth yet endure poverty and hardship oneself while bestowing gifts upon others is the foremost difficult practice.
To be able to open one's own mind and bestow upon others those objects of affection for which one feels extreme attachment—
this is the second difficult practice.
To bestow upon others the wealth acquired through extreme hardship is the third difficult practice.
Fourth, regarding "all doors":
First, one's own property;
second, what has been obtained from others;
third, giving to relatives, to those who provide support, and to beloved servants.
Fourth, giving to others who come seeking;
fifth, the giving of a noble person (satpuruṣa).
Briefly stated, there are five characteristics [of this latter].
One gives with pure faith;
one gives with reverence;
one gives with one's own hand.
Giving at the appropriate time;
giving without harming or distressing others.
Sixth, giving in every respect:
There are thirteen characteristics:
first, non-reliance;
second, vastness.
Third, joy; fourth, repetition;
fifth, the field as a vessel.
Sixth, those who are not fit vessels;
seventh, all things; eighth, all places.
Ninth, at all times;
tenth, faultless;
eleventh, sentient beings as objects.
Twelfth are the gifts of regional products;
thirteenth are the gifts of wealth and grain.
First, regarding the giver who fulfills requests, there are eight characteristics.
First, deficiency in food and drink;
second, deficiency in vehicles;
third, deficiency in clothing.
Fourth, deficiency in ornaments;
fifth, deficiency in requisites;
sixth, deficiency in ointments, perfumes, and garlands.
Seventh, they are destitute of a home;
eighth, they lack light,
yet to those who beg, one gives light.
The seven preceding [categories] are to be understood according to this principle. Eighth, regarding the giving that brings happiness in this world and the next,
there are briefly nine aspects.
There are three kinds of wealth:
first, giving gifts with objects that are exquisite, pure, and in accordance with the Dharma;
second, giving gifts while subduing the defilement of stinginess.
Third, one practices giving while subduing the impurities of hoarding.
There are three kinds of fearlessness:
first, rescuing others from the fear of lions, tigers, wolves, and the like.
Second, rescuing from the fear of kings and bandits;
third, rescuing from the fear of water, fire, and so forth.
There are three kinds of the gift of Dharma.
First, teaching the Dharma without error;
second, teaching the Dharma in accordance with reason;
third, exhorting others to train in the precepts.
These nine aspects enable sentient beings to attain happiness in this world and the next:
material gifts and fearlessness for this world,
and the gift of Dharma for the next world.
The nine kinds of pure giving have ten characteristics:
first, giving without lingering attachment;
second, giving without grasping.
Third, non-accumulation;
fourth, non-exaltation;
fifth, non-reliance.
Sixth, non-retrogression;
seventh, lack of inferiority;
eighth, absence of turning away.
Ninth, not hoping for gratitude;
tenth, not seeking karmic maturation (vipāka),
because one gives swiftly without delay.
Because they do not falsely cling;
because they give immediately without hoarding;
and because they are humble rather than seeking victory over others.
Because it is not based on reputation;
because it is free from regret due to its vastness and lack of self-deprecation;
and because it is the giving of excellent and sublime things.
Because one gives with equal compassion toward both enemies and kin;
because one gives out of pity without seeking recompense;
and because one does not hope for future results.
Regarding the nine gates of ethical discipline (*śīla*):
first, the gate of essential nature (*svabhāva*) has four types.
The first is formal undertaking from another (*parataḥ samādāna*).
Second, the thoroughly pure intention;
third, restoration to purity after having committed an offense;
fourth, profound respect and focused mindfulness.
There is no transgression,
because one has received [the precepts] from another and possesses outward shame (*apatrāpya*).
With a well-purified intention,
because one has committed an offense out of a lack of internal shame,
one returns to purity through focused mindfulness.
There is no initial transgression due to two causes and conditions; thus,
one is free from all remorse.
The first two serve as the basis because they give rise to shame and remorse; it is by means of shame and remorse that [the subsequent stages arise].
One is able to guard ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because one is able to guard it,
one is free from all regret (*kaukṛtya*).
Furthermore, the first two are the actual dharmas,
while the latter two are induced by the former two.
Moreover, the first two and the fourth are capable of preventing destruction.
Having committed an offense, one restores it to purity; having committed an offense, one emerges from it.
Possessing these four merits, one is able to benefit both oneself and others.
For the sake of bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings,
and out of compassion for all people and devas in the world;
second, regarding the "all-encompassing precepts," there are two kinds.
These refer to the precepts for the laity and the precepts for those who have gone forth;
these two categories briefly comprise three, which are the three groups of precepts (triskandha-śīla).
Regarding the three types of difficult-to-practice ethical discipline, there are briefly three kinds.
The first refers to those bodhisattvas who, currently possessing great wealth and superior lineage, are able to renounce them.
To uphold the pure bodhisattva precepts is called the first difficulty;
this is especially so when one encounters a sudden crisis.
Even at the cost of losing one's life,
one would not allow even the slightest deficiency in the precepts one has received,
let alone a full violation.
This is called the second difficulty:
to abide constantly in right mindfulness throughout all activities, whether walking, standing, or attending to mental objects.
Always remain free from negligence;
until the end of life, do not commit even a minor transgression,
let alone a grave one.
This is called the third difficulty.
Regarding the fourth, the morality of all doors, there are briefly four types:
first, the morality of formal undertaking.
Second, the morality of natural disposition;
third, the morality of habitual practice;
fourth, the morality associated with skillful means.
"Right reception" refers to receiving the previously received threefold pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada-viśuddha-śīla*).
"Original nature" refers to...
Abiding in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
they are by nature benevolent and virtuous;
their two types of action— of body and speech— constantly proceed in a state of purity.
Those who have practiced habitually cultivate the three kinds of pure ethical discipline for many lifetimes;
they take no pleasure in the manifestation of any unwholesome dharmas and feel deep revulsion toward such unwholesome dharmas.
One should joyfully cultivate wholesome dharmas and develop a profound sense of aspiration and admiration for them;
this is what it means to be "concordant with the precepts."
Because one constantly engages in virtuous actions toward all sentient beings by relying on the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
there are five types of the ethical discipline of a true person (*satpuruṣa-śīla*). Briefly stated, these five are as follows.
That is to say, bodhisattvas themselves possess ethical discipline (*śīla*),
encourage others to receive the precepts,
and praise the merits of ethical discipline.
Upon seeing those of like dharma,
they feel profound joy; even if such persons should commit transgressions, [they do not harbor ill will].
One should repent and eliminate [faults] in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the sixth, the morality of all aspects:
to state it briefly, it is as follows.
There are six kinds and seven kinds.
Regarding the six kinds:
first is the precept of dedication.
Because it is dedicated toward great enlightenment;
second, the vast and extensive precepts,
because they comprehensively encompass all points of training.
Third, the precepts that are blameless and a source of joy,
because they avoid the two extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification.
Fourth, the constant precepts.
Because one does not abandon them even for the duration of one’s entire life, it is the fifth: firm ethical discipline.
Because it is not overcome or stolen away by the root and secondary afflictions of gain and honor, it is the sixth: unshakable ethical discipline.
Sixth is the morality associated with the ornaments of ethical discipline (*śīla-alaṃkāra*),
because it is fully endowed with all the ornaments of morality,
as described in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Regarding the seven types:
first is the precept of cessation,
because it involves distancing oneself from all acts such as killing.
Second is the transformation into ethical discipline (*śīla*),
because it encompasses all that is wholesome and brings benefit to sentient beings.
Third is the morality of protection,
because it functions as the morality that follows, guards, and brings about cessation.
Fourth is the morality that is the maturation of the marks of a Great Being.
Fifth, the precept that is the maturation of the higher mind;
sixth, the precept that is the maturation of a desirable realm of rebirth;
seventh, the precept that is the maturation of benefiting sentient beings.
Seventh, regarding those who seek the precepts, there are briefly eight types.
That is to say, various bodhisattvas reflect deeply within themselves:
"Just as I myself desire [to attain them]," and so forth.

May they not inflict upon me the taking of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous chatter; nor may they harm me with hands, clods of earth, staffs, or other such unpleasant contacts.
The same applies to others;
since their requests are not fulfilled,
both parties are dissatisfied.
Having thus reflected deeply on the causes and conditions for the difficulty of life,
one does not manifest toward others the eight types of unpleasant matters that result in the failure to achieve what is sought.
Regarding the morality that brings happiness in this world and the next, there are briefly nine kinds.
This means that for the sake of sentient beings,
bodhisattvas should prohibit what ought to be prohibited and permit what ought to be permitted.
They should be gathered and are rightly gathered;
they should be disciplined and are rightly disciplined.
Within this, the bodhisattva’s two types of action—body and speech—constantly proceed in a state of purity.
These are called the four kinds.
Furthermore, there is the pure ethical discipline that accompanies the remaining five perfections,
which constitutes five kinds.
These are designated as the nine [types of precepts].
Because they are able to bring about peace and happiness for oneself and others in both the present and the future,
they are called the "precepts of happiness in both worlds."
Regarding the nine types of pure precepts, there are briefly ten kinds.
The first is the initial excellent reception of the precepts:
for the sake of *sambodhi*, and not for the sake of one's life.
Second is the precept of not being overly depressed,
because one gives rise to regret and shame when transgressing;
and the precept of not being overly agitated.
Third is the precept of being free from indolence, because one does not indulge in attachment to the pleasures of sleep, reclining, and so forth.
This is because one attains freedom from remorse and shame regarding what arises from improper states.
Fourth, the precept embraced by freedom from all forms of negligence,
because one cultivates the five factors of non-negligence as previously described.
Fifth, the precept of right aspiration.
Being far removed from gain and offerings, and having no desire for rebirth in heaven,
one undertakes the practice for oneself;
thus, the precepts are fully embraced by the six modes of conduct.
Because one correctly manifests the bodily and vocal actions of all modes of conduct in accordance with the Dharma;
and because it is the morality encompassed by the seven forms of pure livelihood,
which is free from all faults of wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like.
Eighth is the precept of avoiding the two extremes,
because it is far removed from the extremes of indulging in suffering and pleasure.
Ninth is the precept of ultimate renunciation.

10. The precept of non-decline regarding what was previously received, because there is no deficiency in its reception. This is because it remains far removed from all views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
One who can thus practice will attain five benefits:
first, being protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions;
second, giving rise to joy at the time of death.
Third, maintaining the precepts constitutes having virtuous friends.
Fourth, the four great treasuries of merit are fulfilled.
Fifth, in both the present and future lives, the precepts become one's very nature.
Regarding the nine gates of patience (*kṣānti*):
first, as for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is either the power of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyā-bala*).
Or, by virtue of one's own nature,
one is capable of enduring enmity and harm through a mind free from defilement.
Because of pure compassion,
one is able to exercise endurance;
this is called its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the second, the patience toward all things:
both householders and renunciants each possess three types of patience,
including the patience of enduring enmity and harm.
The arising of the five thoughts is summarized as in the *Nengduan shu* (Commentary on the *Nengduan jing*).
What is meant by "patience" (*kṣānti*)?
It is to be free from one's own anger and agitation.
One does not retaliate against the enmity of others,
nor does it persist as a latent tendency,
flowing and continuing in an uninterrupted stream.
Therefore, it is called "patience.
Regarding the patience of enduring suffering with equanimity,
there are eight matters.
First, suffering in the place of dependence;
second, suffering in the place of worldly phenomena;
third, suffering in the place of deportment.
The suffering of the four means of attraction;
the suffering of the practice of begging;
and the suffering of diligent exertion.
Seventh is the suffering of the sphere of benefiting others;
eighth is the suffering of the sphere of activity.
There are four types of suffering based on the sphere of reliance.
These are the four requisites, such as food and drink.
There are nine worldly sufferings:
namely, loss, censure, disparagement, suffering, ruin, exhaustion, old age, sickness, and death.
There are four types of suffering regarding deportment,
namely the four modes of deportment.
There are seven types of suffering regarding the gathering of the Dharma.
First, making offerings to the Triple Gem;
second, serving one's elders and superiors;
third, inquiring about and receiving the true Dharma.
Fourth, having received [the teaching], one explains it extensively for others;
fifth, one chants and recites it with a great voice;
sixth, one dwells alone in contemplation and investigation.
Seventh, the śamatha and vipaśyanā subsumed under the cultivation of yoga.
There are seven types of suffering regarding the practice of the mendicant’s way of life:
first, the disfigurement of one's appearance and the renunciation of the secular world.
Second, wearing dyed robes;
third, being restrained in movement and remaining ever vigilant and self-composed;
fourth, relying on others for one's livelihood.
5. For as long as life lasts, one shall beg for alms rather than using long-accumulated stores.
6. For as long as life lasts, one shall abstain from sexual intercourse.

7. For as long as life lasts, one shall abstain from watching or listening to dancing, singing, music, and performances involving actors, as well as from using cosmetics and perfumes, and from wearing garlands and ornaments.
Regarding the patience of resolve through reflection (*cintā-adhimukti-kṣānti*):
it is so called because one is able to produce resolve regarding eight types of objects.
The first is the sphere of the virtues of the Three Jewels.
Second, the locus of the true meaning;
third, the locus of the great supernormal powers of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
fourth, the locus of causes; and fifth, the locus of results.
Sixth, the sphere of the meaning that is to be attained;
seventh, the sphere of one’s own skillful means regarding that meaning;
eighth, the sphere of all that is knowable and all that is to be practiced.
One is well-established in those various stages due to two causes and conditions:
first, because of long-term habitual practice;
second, because of the realization of perfectly pure knowledge.
There are three types of patience regarding difficult practices.
First, one endures the harm inflicted by inferior sentient beings.
This is called the foremost difficulty:
to occupy a position of high authority yet fail to provide benefit to one's own subordinates.
To be able to endure it is called the second hardship:
[enduring] the excessive harm inflicted by sentient beings of low caste or servile status.
Being able to endure [this] is called the third difficulty.
Regarding the fourth, the "all-gates," there are briefly four types.
First, regarding harm done by those who are dear;
second, regarding harm done by enemies;
and third, regarding harm done by those who are neutral.
Fourth, one is able to endure all harmful actions, whether they be inferior, equal, or superior in quality, directed toward oneself or others. Fifth,
the patience of a noble being (*satpuruṣa-kṣānti*) consists briefly of five types.
This means that bodhisattvas first perceive the various benefits of patience;
that is, for a person capable of endurance, in a future life.
There will be few enemies and few estrangements;
there will be much joy and happiness.
One will have no regrets at the time of death;
after the dissolution of the body,
one shall be reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the devas.
Having seen these benefits,
one is personally able to endure and encourages others to practice patience.
Praising the merit of patience,
one feels comforted and rejoices upon seeing those who are able to practice it.
Regarding the six types of patience in all their aspects,
there are six kinds.
The first is the thorough understanding that one does not tolerate unpleasant karmic maturation.
One endures out of fear;
one endures out of a mind of compassion, pity, affection, and friendliness toward living beings;
and one practices patience for the sake of perfecting patience for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Now, those who have left the household life possess the power of patience.
It is not that they do not practice patience;
rather, they cultivate patience by means of receiving the Dharma.
One practices patience because one abides in the nature of the lineage through habitual cultivation;
one practices patience because one perceives all sentient beings as being merely phenomena.
There are seven [types].
That is to say: patience toward all that is harmful,
patience toward all who cause harm,
and patience in all circumstances.
Patience at all times;
patience with the entire body,
because of not striking others.
Patience in speech consists in not uttering what is unpleasant;
patience in mind consists in not being provoked to anger.
There are briefly eight types of patience in fulfilling requests.
Regarding those who come seeking from him while suffering in various states of existence,
he is able to endure their importunity;
even toward sentient beings of extremely violent nature and those who commit the highest grades of evil karma, he remains patient.
Compassionate patience toward those who violate the precepts:
one practices compassionate patience toward all who transgress the moral rules.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of endurance regarding the hardship of diligent effort:
enduring the hardship of diligently removing the suffering of sentient beings,
and enduring the hardship of seeking the Dharma.
The hardship of practicing with endurance in accordance with the Dharma;
the hardship of enduring while preaching the Dharma to others;
and the hardship of enduring whatever righteous deeds one performs for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the patience for the happiness of this world and other worlds, there are briefly nine types.
That is to say, when bodhisattvas abide in heedfulness,
they are fully capable of enduring all wholesome dharmas.
One is able to endure cold and heat;
one is able to endure hunger and thirst;
one is able to endure mosquitoes and gadflies.
One is able to endure wind and sun;
one is able to endure snakes and scorpions;
one is able to endure toil, weariness, and distress.
Toward sentient beings who have fallen into the suffering of birth, old age, sickness,
and death, one practices patience out of compassion;
in this way, one enables oneself to dwell in happiness in the present life.
It is not overwhelmed or defiled by any evil or unwholesome dharmas;
it can induce the causes and conditions for peace and happiness in future lives,
and it can also enable others to practice the conduct that brings peace and happiness in both worlds.
This is called "happiness in both worlds.
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of pure patience (*kṣānti*).
These refer to the instances when bodhisattvas encounter harmful actions, injuries, or transgressions committed by others.
He never retaliated,
nor did he feel resentment,
nor did he harbor any malice or aversion.
The continuity of his intention is constantly present;
his desire to bring about benefit remains unchanged from beginning to end.
It is not that one benefits others once and then abandons them so as not to benefit them further.
Toward those who harbor enmity, one goes personally to offer an apology;
one never causes another to become weary or disheartened before accepting their apology.
Fearing that they might become weary or grow tired, one should accept [the invitation] as soon as it is declined, and so forth.
Regarding the nine gates of diligence,
the first is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This means that the minds of bodhisattvas are courageous and resolute,
capable of embracing immeasurable wholesome dharmas and bringing benefit,
peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
That which is fervent, uninterrupted, and free from inversion,
as well as the diligence of body, speech, and mind arising therefrom,
is called the intrinsic nature of vigor.
"Everyone" refers to three types each among both householders and those who have left the home life.
The first are those who don the armor.
Second, gathering virtue;
third, benefiting others.
As for "donning the armor":
This means that prior to initiating the vigor of application, bodhisattvas possess a courageous and resolute mind,
having first donned the armor of their vow.
If, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from suffering,
I were to dwell in the hells for as many days and nights as there are in a thousand great kalpas.
One does not realize awakening while in other realms of existence;
even if one were to realize awakening only after the passage of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of times as many eons, [one would still do so].
My courage is likewise free from retreat;
I do not fail to advance in the pursuit of enlightenment,
and having advanced, I am diligent and tireless.
How much more so when the duration is short and the suffering slight;
this is called the armor-like diligence that gathers what is wholesome.
It is capable of performing the six preparatory practices and accomplishing the six perfections.
Furthermore, there are seven types of this:
first, unwavering diligence.
Because one is unshakable by all conceptual constructions, primary and secondary afflictions, heterodox doctrines, and painful contacts,
there is second, firm progress;
because of the application of earnest and respectful practice.
Third is immeasurable diligence,
because it is able to realize all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) through direct experience.
Fourth is diligence associated with skillful means (*upāya*).
Because one thoroughly penetrates the non-erroneous, compliant practice regarding the meaning that is to be attained,
there is fifth, non-erroneous exertion;
for it is induced by the aspiration to realize that meaning.
Sixth is constant progress,
because of uninterrupted application.
Seventh is progress free from pride.
Because it encourages diligence and abandons arrogance,
it serves as the most excellent cause and condition for swiftly realizing unsurpassed enlightenment through all wholesome dharmas.
What is the diligence that benefits sentient beings?
There are eleven of these,
as explained in the Chapter on Precepts (Śīla-varga).
Those [are precepts] and this is diligence (vīrya).
Regarding their mutual distinctions,
there are briefly three types of those who advance through difficult practices.
First, to be perpetually free from thoughts of clothing, food, bedding, and the body,
and to cultivate the good without interruption or indolence,
is called the first difficulty.
To practice such diligence until the end of one's entire lifespan,
never flagging or ceasing at any time,
is called the second difficulty.
It is characterized by the attainment of equanimity and the possession of merit;
it is neither lax nor overly strenuous,
and it is an unerring diligence capable of bringing about meaningful benefit.
This is called the third difficulty.
As for "all gates," there are briefly four kinds.
First, the exertion of advancing by means of the dharma of detachment from defilements; second, the exertion of inducing one's own dharma;
third, the exertion of purifying karma.
Fourth is the increase of progress in wisdom.
Regarding the progress of a virtuous person,
there are briefly five kinds.
First, the exertion of non-abandonment,
because one does not relinquish the application of effort toward all desires;
second, the exertion of non-retrogression.
Because it nurtures and increases that which was previously received,
there is thirdly, progress without inferiority;
one is courageous, fervent, and exerts oneself with diligence over a long period of time.
Fourth is unerring progress,
because it is sustained by skillful means that can bring about meaningful benefit, and because it is free from cowardice and retreat.
Fifth is the application of diligent effort (*vīrya-prayoga*),
because it enables one to swiftly advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding all types of diligence,
there are six kinds and seven kinds,
totaling thirteen kinds.
Sixth, uninterrupted progress,
which means practicing the preparatory application at all times.
Second is earnest progress,
which means being able to cultivate the preparatory applications (prayoga) thoroughly and completely.
Third is the progress of natural outflow (nisyanda).
This means that because it is sustained by the power of prior causes,
there is progress in the four types of application,
as one repeatedly reflects upon and discerns the application toward wholesome qualities.
Fifth is unshakable diligence,
because it cannot be moved by any contact with suffering.
Sixth is diligence that is never contented.
Because one does not find contentment while realizing what is inferior or limited,
there are the five qualities mentioned in the Sūtra, such as "possessing power" and so forth.
What are the seven kinds?
First, there is the application of energy that proceeds together with desire,
because it is continuously nurtured by a fierce and intense aspiration for enlightenment.
Second, there is the application of energy that is associated with equanimity.
The root and secondary afflictions do not defile or entangle the mind;
because they are able to dwell in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and so forth,
this is the third, the progress toward excellence.
If the mind is defiled by root or secondary afflictions and bound by mental fetters,
one should exert diligence as if one's head were on fire, in order to manifest such vigor.
Fourth is the progress of diligent seeking,
because one seeks the fields of knowledge with tireless perseverance.
Fifth is the progress of cultivation and study.
Sixth is the diligence of benefiting others, because it is able to accomplish the practice in accordance with the Dharma within the teachings one has undertaken to train in.
Because one should understand the characteristics of the eleven types previously mentioned,
there is seventh, well-guarded diligence:
all diligence that gives rise to correct application.
Because one guards oneself well and repents according to the Dharma for transgressions,
one should know that there is happiness in both worlds through patience.
Briefly stated, purity is of ten kinds.
First, proceeding in a balanced manner;
second, thorough cultivation;
third, absence of laxity.
Fourth, skillful gathering;
fifth, timely cultivation;
sixth, thorough penetration of all characteristics.
Seventh, non-retrogression;
eighth, not abandoning the yoke;
ninth, equanimity.
The ten dedications that accord with great enlightenment are for the purpose of severing each respective secondary affliction.
One should cultivate the corresponding remedial methods,
such as cultivating the meditation on impurity to sever attachment;
the other cases should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the nine gateways of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
as for its essential nature,
it refers to the bodhisattvas’ prior application of hearing and reflection upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
All that is sublime and wholesome, both mundane and supramundane:
one-pointedness of mind,
the mind’s correct abiding.
Either belonging to the category of śamatha,
or the category of vipaśyanā, or having as its intrinsic nature the meditative concentration of the path of their union.
All those who practice meditative concentration are,
in brief, of two kinds: namely,
the mundane and the supramundane.
Each of these possesses the merit of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that brings about dwelling in happiness in the present life, benefits sentient beings,
and consists of all forms of dhyāna characterized by physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), freedom from faults, and the subsiding of signs (*nimitta*).
It is called "happiness in the present life.
Because it can induce liberation, vows, wisdom, and so forth throughout the ten directions,
it is called "that which induces."
There are eleven kinds of meditative absorption for the benefit of others,
which should be understood as previously described;
that is to say, bodhisattvas rely upon meditative absorption.
He is able to bring about what is beneficial for all sentient beings;
he acts as a companion in their various undertakings and removes their suffering.
He speaks to all sentient beings in accordance with what is reasonable;
he recognizes and repays the kindness of those who have been gracious to him;
and he acts as a savior for those who are terrified.
He is able to dispel sorrow and grief in those who have suffered loss;
he bestows manifold virtues upon those in want;
and he guides all sentient beings, skillfully acting in accordance with their inclinations.
He gladdens those who possess actual virtues by praising them;
he correctly disciplines those who have faults; and for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests supernatural powers.
That which is drawn forth by fear is called "all meditative absorptions" (dhyāna). There are,
in brief, three types of difficult practices.
Having already been able to abide securely in vast, sublime, and most excellent meditative concentration,
to return to birth in the desire realm for the sake of benefiting sentient beings is called the first difficulty.
Relying upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
one is able to give rise to immeasurable bodhisattva samādhis that transcend the two types of objective domains;
this is called the second difficulty.
Relying upon meditative concentration to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is called the third difficulty.
There are four gateways:
first, dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra;
second, dhyāna accompanied by joy (prīti).
The dhyāna accompanied by the three joys;
the dhyāna accompanied by equanimity.
There are five kinds of noble beings.
First, dhyāna free from attachment;
second, that accompanied by loving-kindness;
third, that accompanied by compassion.
Fourth, that which is accompanied by joy;
fifth, dhyāna accompanied by equanimity.
Regarding "in every respect":
There are six types and seven types.
Regarding the six types:
first, wholesome dhyāna.
Second, the transformation of the indeterminate;
third, the category of śamatha;
fourth, the category of vipaśyanā.
Fifth, the correct and thorough reflection on the welfare of oneself and others;
sixth, the meditative absorption that can induce the qualities of supernatural powers and majesty;
as for the "sevenfold" [classification]:
First is that which has names as its object;
second is that which has meanings as its object; third is that which has the signs of tranquility as its object.
Fourth, the object-condition of the sign of exertion;
fifth, the object-condition of the sign of equanimity;
sixth, dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Seventh, they are able to benefit others.
Consequently, there are eight [types of protection] sought:
first, against all poisons, frost, hail, and calamities.
First, the meditative absorption that serves as the basis for pacifying and accomplishing mantra-sorcery;
second, the meditative absorption that can eliminate the various afflictions arising from the disharmony of the elements;
and third, [the meditative absorption] when famines, fire disasters, droughts, and so forth are manifest.
Fourth, he brings relief from fear;
fifth, [he provides aid] to sentient beings who are destitute of food and have fallen into the wilderness.
1. They are able to bestow food and drink.
6. To those beings to be converted who lack wealth, they are able to bestow wealth.
Seventh, they are able to properly admonish and instruct sentient beings who are heedless throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Eighth, they [act] toward all sentient beings in accordance with whatever arises.
One should practice meditative concentration correctly;
there are nine types of meditative concentration that bring happiness in this world and the next.
The first is the meditative concentration of manifesting supernatural powers to discipline sentient beings.
Second, taming sentient beings through the manifestation of prophetic declarations;
third, taming sentient beings through the manifestation of instructions;
fourth, manifesting the miserable realms to those who commit evil deeds.
Fifth, he bestows eloquence upon those who have lost their eloquence.
Sixth, he bestows mindfulness upon those who have lost their mindfulness.
Seventh, he composes and establishes non-erroneous treatises, subtle hymns of praise, and *mātṛkās*.
It can cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
Eighth, regarding the various worldly crafts and occupations,
it is the meditative concentration that can produce the means of livelihood and resources that lead to meaningful benefit, being able to create them accordingly.
Ninth, for the sake of temporarily pacifying the manifold sufferings of those sentient beings to be converted who have been born in the evil destinies,
he emits great rays of light that touch them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Purity is briefly of eleven kinds:
first, purity through mundane purification by being free from the relish for meditative absorption;
second, purity through supramundane purification by being without defilement.
Third, by purification through application;
fourth, by purification through attaining the fundamental state;
fifth, by purification through the excellence of the fundamental state.
Sixth, the purity of mastery in entering and abiding;
seventh, the purity of mastery in relinquishing meditative absorption and subsequently re-entering it;
eighth, the purity of mastery in the supernormal powers and transformations.
Ninth, purity through being free from all dogmatic views;
tenth, meditative concentration and wisdom that are pure and tranquil regarding all afflictive and cognitive obstructions.
Regarding the nine doors:
First is the single intrinsic nature,
which refers to both the capacity to penetrate all that is knowable and the state of having already penetrated all that is knowable.
It is the discernment of all phenomena,
which operates by universally taking all five fields of knowledge as its object;
it is the very nature of wisdom.
There are two kinds of "all":
namely, the mundane and the supramundane.
Each of these has three types.
First, the wisdom that is able to realize and penetrate the reality of the objects of knowledge;
second, the wisdom that is able [to engage] with the five fields of knowledge as they have been described and within the three collections.
The wisdom of skill in certainty;
the wisdom that can accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings;
and the wisdom of difficult practices, which is of three kinds.
The wisdom that is able to know the profound dharma of selflessness is called the foremost difficulty;
the wisdom that is able to comprehend the skillful means for taming sentient beings [is likewise difficult].
This is called the second difficulty.
To possess unobstructed wisdom that thoroughly understands all objects of knowledge is called the third difficulty.
The "gateways to all" are, in brief, of four kinds;
within the two Piṭakas,
they consist of the two types of wisdom arising from hearing and reflection.
Wisdom that follows through with what ought to be done,
wisdom that ceases what ought not to be done,
and immeasurable wisdom pertaining to the stage of meditative absorption (samāhita-bhūmi) which is encompassed by the power of cultivation.
There are five types of wisdom for a virtuous person:
first, the wisdom accumulated through hearing the true Dharma;
second, the wisdom accompanied by correct internal mental attention.
Third, wisdom that operates in conjunction with the skillful means of practicing for the benefit of oneself and others;
fourth, wisdom that is well-determined regarding all phenomena;
fifth, wisdom that abandons afflictions.
Furthermore, there is another formulation: first, subtle wisdom,
because it penetrates the nature of things as they are (yathāvadbhāvikatā) regarding all that is to be known.
Second is the wisdom of thorough preparation,
because it penetrates the nature of all that can be known as it exists;
third is innate wisdom.
Because it is accumulated through the provisions of wisdom from previous lives,
the fourth is the wisdom that possesses the teachings;
it is able [to engage] with all Buddhas and the assembly of bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages.
Fifth, they possess realized wisdom,
because it is sustained from the stage of pure intention up to the ultimate stage.
All-encompassing [knowledge] consists of six and seven;
the "six" refers to the four noble truths, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising—these are called the six types of wisdom.
The "seven" refers to the dharma-knowledge.
Subsequent knowledge,
conventional knowledge,
and the knowledge of supernormal powers.
The wisdom of characteristics; the wisdom preceded by the ten powers;
and the wisdom of the correct principle among the four principles.
There are eight kinds of seeking wisdom.
First is the knowledge of the different categories of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*), which refers to the unimpeded wisdom regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Second, the knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena;
third, the knowledge of the etymological explanations of phenomena;
fourth, the knowledge of the distinctions among the categories and phrases of phenomena.
That is, the three types of unimpeded analytical knowledge;
fifth, the bodhisattva’s wisdom that completely subdues the arguments of others;
and sixth, the bodhisattva’s wisdom that fully establishes one's own arguments.
Seventh is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that takes as its primary concern the management of all correct instruction regarding family affairs and property.
Eighth is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that thoroughly understands all various worldly administrative duties of kings.
There are nine types of happiness pertaining to the two worlds.
These refer to the bodhisattvas' wisdom that is well-purified and well-established regarding the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā),
and their wisdom that is well-purified but not established regarding the other four sciences (vidyā-sthāna).
All bodhisattvas rely upon such well-cultivated, clear, and pure wisdom regarding the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) as their basis,
for the sake of those sentient beings to be converted who are ignorant, negligent, or lacking in fortitude, and who are diligently applying themselves to correct practice.
According to their respective order,
there are ten purities of wisdom that manifest, instruct, encourage, and console.
Regarding the true meaning, there are two types of wisdom:
namely, that which pertains to the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and that which pertains to the nature of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
Regarding the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*), there are also two types of wisdom.
This means that because one grasps the correct cause and effect,
there are two types of wisdom regarding the meaning of appropriation (*upādāna*):
namely, the wisdom that understands, as they truly are, both the inverted and the non-inverted.
Regarding the meaning of skillful means, there are two types of wisdom,
because one knows as it truly is what should and should not be done.
Regarding the meaning of the ultimate, there are likewise two types of wisdom.

This means that because one understands defilement and purity as they truly are, the five characteristics are called the gates of the *pāramitās*. As stated in the fifty-seventh [fascicle], section seventy-five:
"The various forms of giving possessed by bodhisattvas are, in brief, of five kinds."
When endowed with these merits, one attains inclusion among those who have reached the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
First is non-attachment;
second is freedom from longing.
Third, faultlessness;
fourth, non-conceptuality;
fifth, dedication.
One should know that it is the same for generosity, ethical discipline,
and so forth. "Unattached" means [being free from attachment] regarding all types of factors that obstruct generosity and the other perfections.
"Being without obstruction and without attachment" refers to [the absence of these] regarding existence with its defilements and their fruits.
The mind is without attachment.
Regarding "being without fault":
this refers to being far removed from all types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as [excessive] giving and so forth.
"Non-conceptual" means not observing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) regarding giving and so forth.
"Dedication" means...
This means that one attains the fruit of bodhi through all practices such as giving and so forth, having thoroughly understood each of the preceding nine gates.
Regarding the seven aspects of the gate of purification for giving and so forth, the seventy-fourth [fascicle] states: "The seven aspects of the gate of purification for giving and so forth."
The generosity practiced by a bodhisattva becomes pure through seven aspects,
namely: purity of giving.
Purity of precepts,
purity of view,
and purity of mind.
Purity of speech,
purity of wisdom,
and purity from defilements.
Each possesses ten characteristics.
Regarding the first, the ten characteristics of purity:
the first is the vast giving.
That is to say, because there are many distinctions;
second, the gift of equality,
because there is no deficiency in the Saṃgha.
Third is giving at the appropriate time,
because it accords with what [the recipient] desires.
Fourth is excellent giving.
Because it is complete with [excellent] form and so forth,
it is the fivefold pure gift;
for it is not defiled by being mixed with impure things.
Sixth is giving in accordance with the Dharma,
because it is associated with the absence of fault.
Seventh is giving according to one's inclination.
That is to say, it is because [the gift] accords with what the seeker loves and delights in;
it is the eighth, the gift of benefit,
because it accords with what is appropriate for them.
Ninth, giving that is either sudden or gradual,
depending on the observation of the seeker;
tenth, uninterrupted giving.
Because it is without interruption.
Regarding the ten aspects of the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*):
first, one practices giving by bestowing whatever wealth and goods have been acquired through the exertion of diligent effort.
Second, giving things obtained through the strength of one's own arms;
third, giving things free from defilement and impurity;
fourth, giving in accordance with the Dharma.
Fifth, giving obtained in accordance with the Dharma;
sixth, giving that pacifies and eliminates all evils;
seventh, giving by means of subduing and regulating the sense faculties.
8. Giving with earnest respect;
9. Giving with one’s own hands;
10. First bestowing kindness and support upon one’s own servants and attendants.
Thereafter, when bestowing gifts upon those who come seeking them,
one perceives ten signs of purity:
first, not conceptualizing "I am able to practice giving."
Second, one does not give by measuring others according to one's own standards.
Third, one does not give while observing whether others will repay the gift.
Fourth, one does not give while observing whether there will be wealth and happiness in the future.
Fifth, giving without regard for the absence of fruit;
sixth, giving without regard for the dissimilar fruit of the gift;
seventh, giving without regard for the inverted fruit of the gift.
8. Not giving while regarding the act of killing as a companion to the gift;
9. Not giving while regarding extraordinary transformations or auspicious signs as the cause;
10. Not giving for the sake of reputation or praise.
Regarding the ten aspects of the purity of mind:
first, giving with a compassionate heart;
second, the jewel-like mind.
That is to say, regarding giving:
third, giving with a mind of threefold equanimity;
fourth, giving with a mind that has subdued its defilements.
Fifth is giving with a joyful mind,
which occurs by way of seven aspects;
first, regarding future supplicants.
First, because they give rise to a heart of joy;
second, because as soon as they see those who have come seeking,
they immediately develop pure faith.
Third, because one gives rise to a mind of joy at the time of right giving; fourth,
because one gives rise to a mind of tranquil concentration.
Fifth, because of generating a mind free from attachment;
sixth, because of generating a mind free from affliction;
seventh, because of generating a mind free from regret after giving.
Sixth is giving with a mind of patience,
because of being free from weariness.
Seventh is giving to those who cause harm with a mind of loving-kindness.
Eighth, with a mind of compassion, one gives to those who suffer;
ninth, with a mind of sympathetic joy, one gives to those who possess merit;
tenth, with a mind of equanimity, one gives to friends and relatives.
Regarding the ten aspects of purity of speech:
first, one freely allows the solicitor to choose from the objects to be given.
Second, when they arrive, one should welcome them with the words "Welcome.
Third, one should avoid frowning.
He looked upon them with an even gaze and spoke first with a smile;
fourthly, he offered mutual consolation through gentle words.
Fifth, immediately following this, one says, "I shall bestow upon you desirable wealth.
Sixth, one actually utters the words of giving.
Seventh, if the other person should obstruct it.
Eighth, one refrains from uttering coarse words when distributing [alms].
Ninth, one does not revile or disparage beggars.
Tenth, if there are no items to give...
10. When begging, one never rebukes or mocks the solicitor face-to-face,
causing them to change countenance or feel ashamed.
Regarding the ten aspects of the purification of wisdom:
first, the purification of wisdom by means of giving;
second, the purification of wisdom by means of the petitioner.
Third, by means of the wisdom regarding the objects of giving;
fourth, by means of the wisdom regarding the practice of giving;
fifth, by means of the wisdom regarding maturing sentient beings through giving.
Sixth, by means of the wisdom of skillful means;
seventh, by means of the wisdom regarding the faults of desires;
eighth, by means of the wisdom that removes defilements.
Ninth, by the wisdom that encompasses distancing oneself from [unwholesome] friends;
tenth, by the purity of the wisdom of concealing the six directions.
Regarding the purity of the wisdom of giving:
Because one has thoroughly understood the essence and characteristics of the terminology for giving;
because the seeker’s wisdom is pure;
and because one dwells in the perception of the field of merit.
Regarding the wise person who gives material goods:
they are skillful in crafts and occupations, and are thus able to quickly accumulate goods for the purpose of giving and so forth.
As for their application:
Because one must not cause those who seek [the Dharma] to experience weariness and the like,
the wise one skilled in means instructs them to practice generosity and other virtues.
One eliminates fourteen types of defiled karma by being embraced by wise friends who distance one from evil associates; thus,
one practices giving while remaining far from the four types of bad friends and drawing near to the four types of virtuous friends.

"Concealing the wise ones of the six directions" means that one practices the giving of gifts while concealing these six directions; these three successive gates are as described in the "Peaceful Practices" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the ten aspects of defilement and purity:
First, being free from the defilement of laziness;
second, being free from the defilement of greed;
third, being free from the defilement of hatred.
Fourth, it is free from the defilement of delusion.
Fifth, it is free from the defilement of hindrances; there are four such hindrances:
first, lack of familiarization.
Second, deprivation;
third, indulgence;
fourth, observing the fruit.
This is free from the stain of irrationality.
Sixth is the distribution of the six perfections;
seventh is through the perfection of giving.
This freedom from diminished stains is twofold:
first, the perfection of the objective;
second, the perfection of the intention.
There are seven types of perfection of activity:
first, the gift of material wealth;
second, the gift of a kingdom.
Third, giving to sentient beings;
fourth, giving ornaments;
fifth, giving dwellings.
Sixth, the dwelling place of giving.
Seventh, giving one’s own body.
Eighth, giving through purity.
It is free from the stains of impurity by means of ten kinds of purity,
namely: non-attachment, non-grasping, and so forth.
Ninth, giving that is well-examined is free from the defilement of unwholesome wisdom;
that is to say, it consists in examining the gift itself and examining the intention.
One observes its field.
One who observes things observes the excellence of their function and accumulation.
One contemplates the superior function of giving because it benefits others; one contemplates the four aspects of the underlying intention.
The intentionality that is unerring regarding causes;
the intentionality that is free from attachment regarding results;
and the intentionality that gives rise to compassion.
With a mind of resolute intent perfected in wisdom,
one contemplates five characteristics of the field:
first, that alms may be obtained by begging in this place.
Second, in this situation, having already begged for alms, they further become destitute;
third, in this situation, having already become destitute, they furthermore lack a protector;
fourth, in this situation, lacking a protector, they furthermore commit evil deeds.
Practice.
Fifth, although these [qualities] may not be present in this case, one still engages in practice.
Tenth, possessing the virtue of skillful means, one practices generosity while remaining free from the stains of the faults of lacking skillful means.
That is to say: the habituation of generosity; disregard for body and life; compassion for sentient beings;

the knowledge of the true meaning; resolute conviction in unsurpassed enlightenment; instruction; the power of compulsion; endurance in adverse circumstances; the arising of gratitude and requital; and supernormal powers.
The Section on the Seven Non-Fields to Whom One Should Not Give. There are seven non-fields to whom one should not give.
First, the beggar who is extremely violent and wicked.
First, having previously caused harm, one seeks something from those very ones who have become objects of enmity;
second, though exhorted to perform wholesome deeds, one ultimately fails to attain them;
third, with a corrupted and defiled mind, one begs and solicits for things that are themselves defiled.
Fourth, they beg out of a desire to cause harm and vexation.
Fifth, the beggar may be a māra himself,
or one possessed by a māra, begging in an improper place.
Sixth, begging from one's parents or anyone else for something that is not an object fit for giving.
Seventh, being able to act in a way that is meaningless.
Regarding the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as they cross over through the nine gates: the verses on the four means of attraction through the nine gates are as previously traversed.

The nature of loving speech consists in always delighting in speaking words that are pleasing to the ears, truthful, in accordance with the Dharma, and conducive to the welfare of all sentient beings;
this constitutes the essential nature of loving speech.
Regarding all pleasant speech,
there are briefly three kinds:
first, speech that offers consolation and encouragement.
One should always remain free from frowning when facing sentient beings;
first uttering kind words,
one should relax the countenance and look upon them with a steady gaze.
Smiling first, one should inquire whether they are at ease and auspicious,
or whether their various elements are in harmony.
Sometimes they inquire whether one has been joyful day and night;
sometimes they command one to come forward, saying "Welcome.
Through such signs, they offer consolation and inquiry to sentient beings.
Second is the speech of celebration and joy.
By means of this speech,
when one sees that sentient beings' wives, children, wealth, or grain are flourishing and they themselves are unaware of it, [one speaks to inform them].
One should express joy by awakening to what is appropriate;
or, knowing that faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment,
and wisdom have increased, one likewise rejoices.
Third, the speech that provides supreme benefit:
this refers to speech that accords with the Dharma teachings in which all aspects of excellence are perfected,
and which brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Constantly manifesting benefit through words of supreme advantage—
this constitutes "loving speech that is difficult to practice.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds.
Toward those who would harm them— whether enemies or evil associates—
with a virtuous and pure mind, free from defilement,
they deliberate and speak to them as before with the three words.
This is called the foremost difficulty:
to have no doubt or hesitation in one's mind regarding those sentient beings who are of the highest degree of delusion and dull faculties.
Having reflected upon it, he expounds various teachings for others;
he undertakes this labor with a vow,
grasping it correctly, in accordance with reason, in accordance with the Dharma, and in accordance with what is wholesome.
This is called the second difficulty:
[to encounter] sentient beings who, toward their preceptors, instructors, elders, and true fields of merit, act with flattery, guile, and deception, and who practice evil deeds.
Without a mind of resentment or ill will,
he reflects and speaks to them as before with these three words.
This is called the third difficulty.
There are four types of speech regarding all gateways.
The first is that of one who wishes to sever all hindrances and proceed toward the wholesome.
For those who have previously performed the preparatory rites, he explains them;
for those whose minds are well-trained through the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*),
he explains the sublime Dharma associated with the progressive realization of the Four Noble Truths and so forth.
Third, regarding those householders and renunciants who are largely heedless:
one should provide them with unerring admonition and instruction, employing skillful means to cause them to emerge from heedlessness and to abide in heedfulness.
Fourth, for those who have many doubts regarding all phenomena,
he expounds the treatises on the correct Dharma and provides definitive analysis in order to cause them to be free from doubt in the future.
The loving speech of a virtuous person consists briefly of five kinds,
which they are able to speak for the sake of those to be converted:
[they explain] the causal and conditional dharmas of the Tathāgatas and all Bodhisattvas.
There is the dharma of renunciation;
there is the dharma of reliance;
there is the dharma of courageous resolve.
There is a method of supernormal transformation (*ṛddhi-pāda*). If the Dharma taught is established with a cause for its basis,
it is called "having a causal basis" (*sahetuka*).
If there is a violation of what has been taught regarding the training one has undertaken,
the provision of a means for restoration to purity is called "having an escape."
If the Dharma that is taught is subsumed within the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*),
and the establishment of the correct practice of the Dharma and Vinaya is unerring,
it is called "having a basis."
If the Dharma taught can correctly manifest the practice of non-retrogression from all suffering,
it is called "possessing courageous resolve.
If the Dharma taught performs the three types of miraculous transformations, [it is called "possessing skillful means"].
Everything spoken never goes to waste; this is called a supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Loving speech of every kind consists of six types and seven types.
Regarding the six types:
first, permitting affectionate speech when it concerns teachings that should be heard;
second, prohibiting that which concerns teachings that should be restrained.
Third, the teaching that elucidates all phenomena;
fourth, the teaching that elucidates the non-erroneous characteristics of phenomena;
fifth, the teaching that elucidates the non-erroneous terminology used to explain phenomena.
Sixth is the exposition of the distinctions in the categories of the phrases of the non-erroneous Dharma.
Regarding the seven types:
first is consoling and affectionate speech.
Second, rejoicing; third,
in regard to all requisites for other sentient beings, performing all actions with only slight desire.
Furthermore, even toward those who have attained right view and possess only meager desires,
he extensively employs loving speech;
and with the four bases of sympathy, he comforts those afflicted by various fears.
Fifth, it is comprised of teaching in accordance with reality;
sixth, for the purpose of causing others to emerge from unwholesome states and abide in wholesome states,
one correctly censures them regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Seventh is the pleasant speech of requesting others who possess power and capacity to provide benefit;
this results in eight [types of speech],
namely, the arising of the eight noble modes of speech based upon the four pure modes of speech.
The four pure modes of speech refer to the four types of wholesome vocal karma.
The eight noble modes of speech refer to saying "I have seen" when one has seen, and so forth.
There are nine [factors] for happiness in both worlds.
First, preaching the True Dharma severs the sorrow and anxiety of difficulties regarding one's kinsmen through affectionate speech.
Second, preaching the True Dharma severs the sorrow and anxiety of difficulties regarding wealth and status.
Third, preaching the True Dharma severs the sorrow and anxiety of difficulties regarding freedom from illness.
Fourth, preaching the true Dharma severs the manifold sufferings arising from difficulties regarding pure ethical discipline.
Fifth, preaching the true Dharma severs the manifold sufferings arising from difficulties regarding right view.
Sixth, preaching the true Dharma praises the perfection of pure ethical discipline.
Seventh, preaching the true Dharma to praise the perfection of right view;
eighth, preaching the true Dharma to praise the perfection of proper conduct;
ninth, preaching the true Dharma to praise the perfection of right livelihood and kind speech.
Pure loving speech has twenty kinds, as previously described in the Chapter on Powers (Balapatala).
Its intrinsic nature is beneficial conduct (arthacaryā).
By means of that pleasant speech,
one demonstrates the correct principle to all sentient beings.
According to what is appropriate for each case,
regarding all that is to be learned, they practice in accordance with the meaning and benefit, practicing the Dharma in conformity with the Dharma.
Abiding in such conduct with a mind of compassion and a mind free from attachment,
one exhorts, tames, settles, and establishes others;
this is briefly termed its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*) is, in brief, of two kinds:
first, beneficial conduct that brings to maturity those sentient beings who are not yet mature;
second, beneficial conduct that brings to liberation those sentient beings who have already been matured.
Furthermore, there are three doors:
first, the practice of beneficial conduct that encourages others toward benefits in the present life;
second, the practice of beneficial conduct that encourages others toward benefits in future lives.
Third, there is the beneficial conduct of exhorting others toward benefits in both the present and the future.
Regarding the beneficial conduct of exhorting others toward benefits in the present life:
this refers to exhorting them to gather, protect, and increase their wealth and status through the practice of Dharma and virtuous qualities.
By this, one is able to attain great renown and happiness in the present life;
through the enjoyment of requisites, one dwells in comfort,
and is exhorted toward the benefits of future lives to benefit those who practice.
He correctly exhorts them to renounce wealth and status to enter the pure life of homelessness,
and to subsist by the practice of mendicancy;
through this, they will certainly attain happiness in future lives.
Without necessarily seeking personal happiness in the present life,
one encourages practitioners toward benefit in both the present and the future,
providing correct exhortation to those who are either householders or renunciants.
By practicing the gradual stages of cultivation, one proceeds toward the departure from desire;
through this, one is able to attain pliancy in the present life and subsequently be reborn in the Pure Heavens,
or else attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of no-remainder.
Beneficial conduct that is difficult to practice is briefly of three kinds:
beneficial conduct that can be practiced toward sentient beings by means of superior roots of virtue not previously practiced.
This is called the foremost difficulty,
because it is difficult to encourage [others] toward it.
It refers to the conduct for the benefit of sentient beings who possess virtuous causes present before them, who are attached to vast wealth, status, and perfected requisites.
This is called the second difficulty.
Because of the proliferation of extensive negligence and attachment,
he performs beneficial deeds for those sentient beings among the various non-Buddhists who are attached to their original heterodox paths and hold wrong views and wrong conduct.
This is called the third objection.
It arises because they are deludedly attached to their own school and because they harbor hatred and opposition toward the true Dharma and Vinaya.
There are four types of beneficial conduct regarding all gateways:
encouraging sentient beings who lack faith to have faith,
and encouraging sentient beings who violate the precepts to observe the precepts.
One encourages beings of impaired wisdom in wisdom;
one encourages beings who are stingy in generosity.
There are, briefly, five kinds of beneficial conduct for virtuous persons.
They encourage sentient beings toward the ultimate truth;
they encourage them at the appropriate time;
and they encourage them in the gathering of sublime meanings.
One encourages sentient beings with gentleness;
one encourages sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness.
There are six or seven kinds of beneficial conduct in every respect.
The sixth refers to those sentient beings who should be correctly gathered and are thus correctly gathered;
who should be correctly disciplined and are thus correctly disciplined;
and whose resentment toward the holy teaching is removed.
Those who dwell in the middle are led to enter the holy teaching;
those who have already entered the holy teaching are brought to maturity;
and those who have already matured are led to attain liberation.
The seventh refers to guarding and nurturing the provisions for virtue according to the beings to be converted,
whether in the Lesser Vehicle or the Great Vehicle,
or in seclusion, or in one-pointedness of mind.
Alternatively, they may be correctly established in the purification of various obstacles, or in the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*);
if there are those with the lineage of the two vehicles, they are correctly established within those two vehicles.
If those of the Mahāyāna lineage are established within the Mahāyāna and subsequently seek to practice for the sake of benefit, there are eight [instances].
That is to say, they see sentient beings who, regarding matters that should inspire shame, are entangled by the fetter of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*).
Through skillful means, he provides instruction and liberation so that they may be freed from those envelopments;
the same applies to the other seven envelopments.
There are nine [types of] happiness pertaining to both worlds.
That is to say, with respect to other sentient beings,
relying on pure bodily action,
one exhorts them to abstain from taking life.
He abstains from taking what is not given.
He abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from all *surā*, *maireya*, and *madana*—intoxicating liquors that are the basis for negligence.
Relying on pure verbal karma,
they exhort others to abstain from all false speech and to abstain from divisive speech.
He abstains from harsh speech and abstains from frivolous chatter;
he relies upon pure mental action.
Exhorting others to abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
There are ten aspects of pure beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
Five of these depend on external purity.
First, conduct that is free from fault;
second, non-reversal;
third, gradual progression.
Fourth, universal application;
fifth, appropriate application:
those who have committed various evil deeds are correctly established within various virtues.
This is called "blameworthy conduct.
Within that which is neither liberation nor the purity of meditative concentration,
one seeks what is falsely claimed to be true liberation.
Seeking to attain the purity of meditative concentration,
one is able to provide correct exhortation therein;
this is called "unwavering practice."
Knowing [the disciples'] inferior,
middling, and superior capacities, he teaches them the lower, middle, and higher dharmas in their respective order;
through instruction and admonition, he causes them to practice gradually.
To encourage all sentient beings— those who act for their own benefit according to their strength and capacity, and those who seek happiness—
to do likewise within those respective categories is called "universal beneficial conduct."
Regarding all sentient beings,
those who can be exhorted through the distinctions in the efficacy of the three grades of wholesome dharmas pertaining to their own welfare,
as well as those who can be exhorted through the distinctions in the efficacy of skillful means.
To provide such exhortation through appropriate skillful means is called "beneficial conduct according to what is suitable.
Based on internal purity, there are five forms of beneficial conduct.
Toward all sentient beings,
he gives rise to vast compassion,
and this resolute intention manifests before him.
Yet he practices beneficial conduct;
regarding the welfare and benefit performed for all sentient beings,
he endures every great suffering and toil.
Yet their minds never grow weary;
they give rise to profound joy and practice beneficial conduct.
Although he manifests as dwelling in the most excellent, supreme, and perfect station of wealth and status, he remains humble,
like a slave or a servant.
Furthermore, it is like a filial son who, though born of a caṇḍāla mother,
has a humble and submissive mind,
free from arrogance and self-clinging.
Yet he practices beneficial conduct toward all sentient beings with a mind free from attachment.
Free from deceit, with genuine compassion,
he practices beneficial conduct.
Toward all sentient beings,
they give rise to a mind of compassion that is ultimately irreversible,
and thereby practice beneficial conduct.
Thus, they collectively constitute ten.
Regarding "common purpose":
it refers to listening to this meaning.
Thereupon, through these roots of goodness,
they are exhorted and taught,
such that [their virtues] are either equal or increased.
He personally undertakes the training and shares the same activities as others,
so that the sentient beings being transformed perceive him as one of their own kind.
One should train with certainty and firm resolve,
never regressing, thinking:
"This will certainly bring me benefit and happiness."
He himself practices what he teaches;
there is no one who practices what they teach while knowing it to be without benefit or happiness.
It is not the case that Bodhisattvas do not act in this way through "sameness of purpose" (sāṃketika).
One may raise this challenge:
"If you do not accept the training yourself,
how can you exhort and instruct others?"
You should receive instruction and admonition from others.
There are bodhisattvas who act as colleagues with others but do not manifest themselves as such;
that is to say, they possess equal power [with others] yet do not manifest it.
There is that which does not share the same activity as others but manifests itself as sharing the same activity with others;
this refers to manifesting an inferior state oneself in order to lead others.
There is also that which shares the same activity as others and likewise manifests itself as sharing the same activity with others.
This means that when he perceives that the roots of goodness of those to be converted are wavering,
he manifests the practice of "common purpose" (samānārthatā) in order to cause them to remain firm.
Whether increasing or equal,
it does not act in concert with others,
nor does it manifest itself.
Regarding "engaging in the same activities with others": this refers to one’s own practice being negligent while abandoning the affairs of others.
Each of these nine doors for attaining fruits—from the aforementioned door of giving up to the door of engaging in the same activities—yields its respective fruit.
If one extensively cultivates all forms of giving and so forth,
and brings them to perfect purity.
If one is fully endowed with these three, they will flow down through the lower gates,
capable of producing the fruit of the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, the vajra-body, and the long endurance of the True Dharma.
Difficult practices can bring about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s marvelous qualities;
through every gateway, one attains the fruit of being the most excellent among sentient beings, honored by gods and humans;
and through the gateway of the virtuous person, one attains the fruit of being the most supreme among all gateways of sentient beings.
The fruit of a body adorned with the marks and signs, encompassed by immeasurable and preeminent merit acquired through all modes;
and the fruit of a gateway for seeking that can evoke the Tathāgata’s seat, the seat of enlightenment, which cannot be disturbed or shaken by Māra.
The gate of the two worlds attains the fruit of the Tathāgata’s most excellent meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*);
the gate of purity brings about the fruit of the Tathāgata’s fourfold purity in all its aspects.
That is to say: purity of the basis,
purity of the object,
and purity of the mind.
Purity of Wisdom.

Regarding the ten karmic actions that result in the retribution of a short lifespan, the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "The boundless, desirable, and faultless superior fruits [of purity]... [Ten karmic actions that result in the retribution of a short lifespan—Ten karmic actions that result in the retribution of a short lifespan. The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* says:
There are ten kinds of karma that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of a short lifespan.
First, personally committing the act of killing.
Second, exhorting others to kill;
third, praising killing;
fourth, rejoicing upon seeing someone kill.
Fifth, wishing for the destruction and extinction of those one hates;
sixth, feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing the destruction of an enemy;
seventh, destroying the fetal development of others.
Eighth, teaching others to destroy [the Dharma].
Ninth, establishing celestial shrines and slaughtering sentient beings.
Tenth, teaching people to engage in warfare and mutually inflict harm upon one another.
The Ten Karmic Gates of the Longevity Retribution: These ten karmas can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of long life.
First, one does not kill oneself;
second, one exhorts others not to kill.
Third, praising the abstention from killing;
fourth, feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing others refrain from killing;
fifth, seeing those who kill and employing skillful means to rescue and exempt them.
Sixth, he consoles the hearts of those facing the fear of death.
Seventh, he bestows fearlessness upon those who see terror.
Eighth, he gives rise to a mind of compassion upon seeing those who are afflicted by illness.
Ninth, seeing various emergencies and hardships, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Tenth, one bestows various foods and drinks upon sentient beings.
Regarding the ten karmic paths of being frequently ill or not being ill: there are ten karmic paths that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of frequent illness.
First, taking pleasure in beating and striking all sentient beings;
second, encouraging others to beat them;
third, praising the act of beating.
Fourth, taking pleasure in striking others;
fifth, harassing one's parents and causing them mental distress;
sixth, harassing the noble and holy ones.
Seventh, seeing an enemy’s illness, one feels great joy in one's heart.
Eighth, seeing an enemy’s illness cured, one feels displeasure in one's mind.
Ninth, providing what is not a remedy for an enemy’s illness.
There are ten instances where one eats again even though previous food has not yet been digested.
Furthermore, there are ten karmic actions that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of freedom from illness.
The first four are the reverse of the preceding four.
Fifth, making offerings to one's parents and all who are ill.
Sixth, visiting and providing care and offerings for the sick among the worthy and holy ones (*ārya*).
Seventh, seeing that an enemy’s illness has been cured, one feels joy in one's heart.
Eighth, seeing those suffering from illness, one bestows excellent medicine upon them and also encourages others to do so.
Ninth, one gives rise to a mind of compassion toward those suffering from illness.
Tenth, one is able to exercise self-restraint regarding food and drink.
Regarding the tenfold gate of the retribution for the beauty or ugliness of karma: there are ten types of karma that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of ugliness.
First, they habitually practice anger;
second, they habitually harbor resentment;
third, they deceive others.
Fourth, they afflict and disturb sentient beings.
Fifth, they lack love and respect toward their parents.
Sixth, they do not give rise to reverence for the noble and holy ones.
Seventh, they plunder the livelihoods and fields of the noble and holy ones.
Eighth, they extinguish the lamp-light at the stupas and temples of the Buddha.
Ninth, upon seeing those who are ugly, they revile, despise, and treat them with contempt.
There are ten habitual evil practices.
There are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of physical beauty:
first, being free from anger.
Second, giving clothing;
third, loving and respecting one's parents;
fourth, honoring the noble and holy ones.
Fifth, to anoint and decorate Buddhist stupas;
sixth, to sweep and sprinkle the halls and buildings;
seventh, to sweep and sprinkle the grounds of the Saṃgha.
Eighth, to sweep and sprinkle the Buddha-stūpas.
Ninth, upon seeing those who are ugly or deformed, not to give rise to contempt or disdain, but to arouse a mind of reverence.
Tenth, upon seeing those who are handsome and upright, to awaken to and understand their past causes.
Ten karmic actions lead to birth in low or high lineages; ten karmic actions cause one to receive the retribution of being born into a low lineage.
First, failing to respect one’s father.
Second, failing to respect one’s mother.
Third, disrespect toward śramaṇas;
fourth, disrespect toward brahmins;
fifth, lack of reverence and protection for one's elders and superiors.
Sixth, not rising to welcome or making offerings to one's teachers and elders;
seventh, not rising to welcome or inviting a venerable person to be seated upon seeing them;
eighth, not honoring the instructions of one's parents.
